now leave the Chair for the House to go into Committee of the Whole on Bill (No. 147) to incorporate the Toronto and Hamilton Railway Company.

Mr. Speaker, it has been represented that some points that have been raised in connection with this Bill were not fully considered by the Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines, and with the permission of the House, if it is agreeable to all parties, I beg to move :
That the order be discharged and that the Bill be referred back to the Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines for further consideration.
speakername: The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS (Hon. James Sutherland).

speechtext: May I ask the hon. minister (Hon. Mr. Sutherland) if the proposition to refer the Bill back has been agreed to by both parties ?
No.

I may say, for the information of the House, that there was considerable difference of opinion as to the merits of this measure. The right hon. leader of the government (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and some of his colleagues received a deputation representing both parties, and the conclusion was reached that the counsel having charge of this measure should present to the government the case in support of the measure and that flve days should be given to those who oppose it to make answer to the case presented on behalf of the promoters. Since that meeting was held, in so far as I am aware, those representing the municipalities opposed to the Bill in its present form have not been heard from, and I want to know if the action that is being taken meets with their concurrence ?

As the hon. gentleman (Mr. Clarke) is aware, the invariable practice on both sides of the House, I think, is to support the report of a standing committee of the House when they have examined a matter that is referred to them by the House. Naturally, we come to the conclusion that they have given the best consideration to the question that is possible to give to it, and we are prepared to give to their report all due consideration. That rule of the House has been invariably observed, except where it has been shown that there has been misrepresentation, or that an important feature of the measure has not been examined. This Bill has been reported by the Railway Committee, but since the Bill has been so reported it has been represented to us that this was a matter which invaded provincial rights. Strong representations, as my hon. friend knows, have 245}
been made to us in that respect. It is difficult to come to a conclusion and to form a judgment upon the point so raised except by a thorough examination and discussion of the Bill itself and the effect of it. We have, therefore, without prejudging the question at all, thought it preferable to have the matter referred back to the Committee on Railways, so as to give an opportunity to all parties to have the matter thoroughly threshed out, and that is the reason we have come to the conclusion that it is better that this motion should be made and the matter again brought to the attention of the Railway Committee. I have received a long memorandum from the city of Toronto upon this subject.
speakername: The PRIME MINISTER (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier).

speechtext: Before the matter is taken up by the Railway Committee, will those who are opposing the Bill in its present shape be communicated with and be given an opportunity of being present so that they may be heard ?
Oh, certainly.
I do not know the views of either party, but I thought the best way to do was to give the parties an opportunity of being heard by the members of this House in the Railway Committee.
Motion agreed to.

On section 11,
Mr. McCARTI-IY. The leader of the opposition suggested that the word ' common ' should be inserted after the words 'amount of such' so as to make it read 'amount of such common stock.' I have consulted the parties interested, and I am prepared to accept the suggested amendment. This amendment would make the clause apply to common stock and not to preferred stock.

In the government Bill there is a class of stock which comes after the government guarantee and which is to be guaranteed by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. Can they issue this stock in payment of the guarantee for that other stock?
Mr. McCarthy. I should think not.
You are quite sure that they cannot.

Get it defined if there is any doubt about it.
Mr. McCarthy. Is there any doubt about it ?

This clause has to be considered" in connection with other proposed amendments, one of which has reference to the power of the company to enter into an agreement with the government for the construction and operation of the line. Then there is a provision in the Bill submitted bv the Prime Minister under which the Grand Trunk Railway Company is to acquire the whole of the common stock of this company. Taking this clause in connection with that provision, what is the effect upon the question of the construction of the railway from Moncton to Winnipeg ? Is it the intention of these three provisions to which I have called at-

tention that this stock shall be issued under some arrangement between this company and the Grand Trunk Pacific and that the Grand Trunk Railway Company shall construct that portion of the railway ? Is that not possible ?

I think not, because this section only applies to any payment for ' plant, rolling stock, docks, elevators, wharfs, warehouses, vessels or materials.' All the common stock is to be held by the Grand Trunk Railway Company, so that during the term of the lease for fifty years it is still in the hands of that company.

Let us see if it can be worked out. We will suppose that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company makes a contract with the government of Canada to construct a line of railway from Moncton to Winnipeg, and sublets that contract to the Grand Trunk Railway Company. I do not know whether that can be done or not. I do not know what the powers of the Grand Trunk Railway Company are in that regard. Under the provisions of this clause this company might allot the whole of the common stock to the Grand Trunk Railway Company as part of the compensation for the construction of that line. I think that is possible.

I submit that it is not possible, because under the contract with the government the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway stock of $25,000,000 is to be acquired and held by the Graud Trunk Railway Company ; so that for fifty years the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway will not be at liberty to allot its stock at all .

That does not quite answer what I have said. I have said that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway make a contract with the government to build this line. There is a provision in the Bill for a transcontinental railway that the Grand Trunk Railway Company shall acquire all the stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. Assuming that the Grand Trunk Railway Company has the power under its charter, it could acquire under the provisions of this Bill the $25,000,000 'of stock of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway in the way I have mentioned. 1 would like to know whether the Grand Trunk Railway Company has power to enter into a contract of that kind ?

The only difficulty I see as to that is that according to my general knowledge of the Grand Trunk Railway Act, that company has no authority to build a railroad at all. I may say that this section Is similar in terms to section 39 of the General Railway Act.

This is far wider. This provides that ' as consideration for rights, powers, and privileges acquired ' the company may issue paid up stock. Under
the Bill introduced by the government, it is provided that the Grand Trunk Railway Company shall take stock in the new undertaking to the extent of $25,000,000. I could not understand where the company could get the money to take that stock. This section enables the new company to allot its stock to the Grand Trunk Railway Company as a payment for the guarantee of the transcontinental railway's bonds, or for the purchase of rolling stock for the new line.
Will the hon. gentleman be good enough to point out the word V Is it in consideration for rights acquired, for powers acquired, for privileges acquired, that they can get that stock ?
Yes.
Under whieh of the words could it be done ?
In consideration for rights, powers and privileges acquired.
Which of the words would cover it ?
Any of them. A privilege is the endorsing of the bonds by the Grand Trunk Railway.

That would not surely be a privilege acquired. How could you call a guarantee given upon tlie second mortgage bonds a privilege acquired by the Grand Trunk Railway ? It would be a liability incurred by the Grand Trunk Railway.
Surely it is a privilege to the company that gets It.
I am sure that if my hon. friend will consider these words iurther, he will change his opinion.

Would it not be under services rendered ? Under this Act of incorporation the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway may Issue paid up stock for the guarantee received from the Grand Trunk Railway on their second-class securities for the purpose of purchasing rolling stock for the two lines.

There must be somewhere in the Act of incorporation authority for the Grand Trunk Pacific to transfer these over to the Grand Trunk Railway or otherwise the Grand Trunk Railway could not take the stock. I do not think they could do it under this clause.

As this amendment covers mine, X beg to withdraw the amendment of which X gave notice.

Does this amendment
affect a tramway which runs outside a municipality 7
It applies to any municipality affected.

The consent of every
muncipality must be obtained. But suppose a road runs between two municipalities, and one of them refuses to give consent, to whom is there an appeal for a redress ?
We have no redress.
It is a remarkable piece of legislation to put a railway company in such a position that if a municipality objects to giving permission, the railway company has no alternative.
This only applies to the branches.
Will the general law in Canada be affected ?

The hon. gentleman will remember that we had quite a long discussion when the Bill'was in committee before, and it was explained that these ropeways and tramways only applied to the province of British Columbia. That is the intention of the promoters of the Bill, and I stated to the committee that that provision was thus confined. The hon. member for Victoria and the hon. member for West Toronto gave notice of amendments, and these amendments were considered, and the power which is sought to be embodied in Mr. McCarthy.
this clause was understood hy them. I see the point made by the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Ingram). In the more thickly or densely populated section of the country it would be proper not to accept the amendment which I moved, but inasmuch as it applies to British Columbia, and the intention being only to run tramways or ropeways to or from a mine, for instance, I do not see that there would be any difficulty on our part. I quite see it might be a precedent that may do harm in the future.
I am not objecting so far as the present Bill is concerned, but in view of the future; I am speaking of this parliament laying down a principle covering the General Railway Act of Canada.

This matter has been discussed again and again in committee. The municipalities must have protection against these insidious attempts to promote legislation in this parliament to override provincial and municipal rights. The hon. gentleman who has charge of this Bill understands the situation exactly. He has consented to an amendment to meet the views I have presented. We must guard against any action, under the guise of general legislation, that will give power to run tramways through the streets of a municipality without its consent. What this company desired was power to construct tramways on the streets and highways of a municipality without its consent. AVill it he contended that the company should have power to run tramways through the streets of any municipality in Canada, if the municipality does not consent ? It strikes me that the power to authorize the operation of tramways belongs to the provincial legislatures, and not to this parliament.

It does not interfere with the main line at all, or their branches. The principle which my hon. friend from West Toronto is advocating so firmly only applies to rope lines to and from the main line of the road.
To all kinds of tram-roads.
It only applies to lines of road in British Columbia. As amended it only applies now to those in British Columbia for the purpose of reaching mines of ore.

Before the amendment to section 26 is carried, I desire to move an amendment to that amendment, of which I gave notice. The object of my amendment is to prevent this company from exercising a power which I do not think has been granted to any other railway company, that is a power to build branch lines from branch lines, and thus extend their operations all over the country. As I read section 11 of the Act, I understand that the Grand Trunk Pacific Rail-

way includes tlie main line and the branches named therein. Now when we read section 2G we find that the company takes power ' to construct, acquire and 'operate tramways or other ways for the transportation of ore and other freight to or from any point on its railway or any branch thereof.''
The hon. gentleman is not reading from my amendment, but he is reading from the original Bill. His point is well taken as to the original Bill, but not as to my amendment.

I will now read the amendment:
The company may construct, acquire and operate ropeways for the transportation of ores and other freight, and also tramways, not exceeding ten miles in length in any one case, to or from any point on its railway or anabranch thereof.
Now it is quite clear to my mind that power is here taken to construct a brand) line ten miles in length and then throw out another branch line ten miles from the first one, and so continuously ; so that practically it is a charter that covers the whole country. Now I think there should be some limitation to bring it within the general scope of what parliament has allowed, simply branch lines ten miles in length from its main line.

The proposed amendment to this section only applies to ropeways or tramways, and they are to be limited to ten miles in length. Such ropeway or ti-amway may start from the main line or from a branch line. Nothing more is asked for, it goes no further. The objection the hon. gentleman now makes is well founded as concerns the original clause, but not as concerns the suggested amendment.

It seems to me this section simply consecrates a principle which has been accepted in the Railway Committee, that tramways should not circulate through streets without permission of the municipality. The objection raised is that this does not give sufficient power to the municipality in case of conflict arising between the municipality and the railway company. I do not think that objection ought to be sustained, because if the municipality lias a decided objection to the circulation of tramways upon its streets, I do not see that we have any power to interfere with the power of the municipality which, as I understand, we want tql establish. Moreover if it only applies to British Columbia for the conveyance of ore, I do not see what objection there can be.

The municipalities are not trying to block the great railway companies ; what they are trying to do is to prevent tramways being forced upon them through a general Railway Act, without their consent. No municipality ever yet tried to block a railway in the manner suggested
here to-day. They have not done it, and until such a case arises, I think we might just as well accept the clause as it is today.

We know now the men we are dealing with and we have the proposal the government made the other day. bo, I am quite in order in going into the whole question, and I am going to do it. The cry of the west to-day is in regard to transportation. The cry of the west is: Help us to move our crops; we have abundant crops, more than can be handled bv existing routes, and wte ask the people of Canada to afford us relief from the present condition of things.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Will the hon. member (Sir. Slaclean) allow me to put the motion?

Yes.
Amendment was read.

As I was saying, Sir. Chairman, tlie cry of the west is'for help to solve the transportation problem. They say : We cannot move oiy freight; there are not sufficient elevators; there is not sufficient rolling stock; in every way things are not as they ought to be, and we appeal to the parliament of Canada for relief. In answer to that appeal a proposition lias been made by the government, and this Bill has been introduced in the House. I do not think this Bill should be allowed to pass, for the reason that neither this Bill nor the proposed measure of the government deals with this difficulty in the right way. What the people want is relief in regard to transportation, and most

of all they want relief by * means of a government-owned railway. The people of Canada say : If we pay for a railway, If we supply all the money to build It, let that railway be our own. In no way let that railway pass from us into the hands of private parties. And this is in accord with the cry of the west for relief from their transportation difficulties, and relief by a road owned and managed by the government. But the proposal involved in this Bill, the proposal brought down by the government gives no immediate relief to the people of the North-west. The proposal is to build a road through the wilds of New Brunswick, a road through the wilds of the Laurentian country in Quebec, a road through the wilds of Ontario, through the so-called clay belt, and so across the prairies and through the mountains to the Pacific coast. Outside of that part of the road in Manitoba and the North-west, there is not a single proposition in the whole scheme that aids in the solution of the transportation problem, or gives relief to the people of the Northwest.
Now, in wbat way can relief be given to the people of the North-west under present circumstances? In one way and one way only, and that is by adopting the principle of government ownership. If the government were alive to the situation, the first thing they would do would be to build a railway to be owned and operated by the government from Port Arthur on Lake Superior to Winnipeg and so into the west. Some years ago when a proposition was made in this House to subsidize very heavily a railway called the Rainy River Railway and now a portion of the Canadian Northern, and owned by Mackenzie and Mann, I appealed to the government to nationalize that road. I pointed out that not only was a large grant being made by the Dominion, but large grants had been made by the province of Manitoba and the province of Ontario, the public moneys thus granted being, as I believed and contended, sufficient to build the road. And, as the public were paying for the road, I appealed to the government to nationalize the work. But they ridiculed the idea. And now we are told we are having government ownership. Within six years of the time when they ridiculed the idea of government ownership, they boast of adopting it. And I must say that the late Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Blair) ridiculed the idea that I then brought forward, but he has sincie seen the light, and I hope he will support me in

If the bon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean) will permit me a word, I think that what he was then proposing was to nationalize all the railways in Canada. I raised no objection to the building of a railway through that country by the government-never in my life.

What I say is that, when the Rainy river proposition went through, and the late Minister of Railways and Canals endorsed it, I appealed to him and to the government to nationalize that road in the interest of the country. At that time I entered into correspondence with Mr. Hays, who had recently come to Canada, and told him that, so far as I could see, the great aim of the Grand Trunk should be to get an entrance into the Canadian North-west, and the way to get in was to make such representations at Ottawa as that the government would throw out these subsidy proposals and would nationalize that road from Port Arthur to Winnipeg, and to permit the Grand Trunk to get into that country. Mr. Hays at that time said he was seized of the idea, but he had other propositions before him and that he must defer dealing with the matter for some time.
How did the bon. member (Mr. Maclean) intend that the Grand Trunk should get into the North-west?
speakername: The MINISTER OF JUSTICE (Hon. Mr. Fitzpatrick).

speechtext:
The Grand Trunk today is at Midland. The Grand Trunk could, to-morrow, by a fleet of steamers, be at Port Arthur. Nationalize the Canadian Northern, as I say, or if necessary, nationalize the Canadian Pacific from Port Arthur to Winnipeg. Do this, and you have solved the problem. You can then extend a government-owned railway out into the prairies, or you can nationalize the Canadian Northern, and so reach through to Manitoba and the North-west Territories, and, shortly, clear across the continent. That is the way to give immediate relief to the North-west. That is the way to give the people cheap transportation. It is simply a matter of nationalizing the ' spout.' Sir William Van Horne very aptly called that portion of the country between Winnipeg and Port Arthur the 'spout,'. and my idea is that that portion at least ought to be nationalized, all other roads should be allowed equal right of way over it, and the tolls should be reasonable. Is there any other way to solve the transportation question except on the principle of ' the King's highway' ? A great mistake was made in England when the railways were first built there by allowing those railways to become private roads. Like any other roads, they should have been retained as 'the King's highway.' The step that was then taken has been deeply regretted, and an effort is now being made in England to retrieve that mistake. We also could have saved ourselves by recognizing the principle of 'the King's highway.' If we had this road from Winnipeg to Port Arthur as a public highway, we could run the Grand Trunk over it, we could run the Canadian Northern over it, wie could run the Canadian Pacific over it, and, best of

all, we could run the Intercolonial over It. We could have the four great systems working for the Canadian North-west, handling the traffic of that country, and, with the competition that would be assured, we should have a lowering of rates.
By way of information, would the hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean) permit me to ask how he would get from Port Arthur to Midland over the Grand Trunk?
For the present, I would get there by a line of boats.
Not otherwise ?
I might go this far- nationalize the Grand Trunk to North Bay, and, if the Canadian Pacific would not make terms, I would nationalize their line from North Bay to Port Arthur.
Then the nationalization of the line would be from Winnipeg to North Bay?
It might be. But the way to give speedy relief is to invite these great railways to a conference, and tell them plainly what we propose.

The Finance Minister said that could not be done without a vote of the House, giving its consent to the committee rising. I said that that would leave the minority in a hopeless position. The Prime Minister and the chairman both now agree with me, that the minority have some rights, and that we can get the opinion of the Speaker without the consent of the House.
If my hon. friend was right the other day he is wrong now.

air. SPEAKER. Mr. Macdonald, of the committee of the Whole, reports that the committee has decided to refer to the Speaker for his decision:	Whether the
Committee of the Whole can discuss the principle of the Bill (No. 64) by reason of an amendment to section 1 of the Bill having been offered.
At the outset I may say that, generally speaking, the principle of a Bill should be discussed on the second reading thereof, but that rule is somewhat different in the case of private Bills and public Bills. In the case of public Bills, it is not in order to discuss in committee the general merits of a Bill on a particular clause ; but, in the ease of private Bills, the rule, as stated by May, is as follows :
The second reading corresponds with the same stage in other Bills, and in agreeing to it. the House affirms the general principle, or expediency of the measure. There is, however. a distinction between tine second reading of a public, and of a private Bill, which should not be overlooked. A public Bill being founded on reasons of state policy, the House, in agreeing to its second reading, accepts and affirms those reasons; but the expediency of a private Bill, being mainly founded upon allegations of fact, which have not yet been proved, the House, in agreeing to its second reading, affirms the principle of the Bill, conditionally, and subject ro the proof of such allegations before the committee.
With regard to this Bill, its principle was considered when the motion was made in committee of the whole for the adoption of the preamble of the Bill. In the case of private Bills, the principle is supposed to be contained in the preamble, and when the preamble has been declared carried, then, according to my view, the principle of the Bill cannot be further discussed in committee. The Committee of the Whole is now considering clause 1 of the Bill, which contains the names of the incorporators, and on that clause it is not in order to discuss the principle of the Bill.
Mr. Speaker then left the Chair, and the House resumed in Committee of the Whole.

Mr. Chairman, in order to get myself before the committee-and I

accept the ruling that has been given-I beg to move that you tlo now leave the Chair, and, on that motion, I propose to discuss the general question. So, we have only lost forty minutes. I wish to discuss the whole question involved in this Bill, particularly in view of the fact that Sir Charles Rivers-Wilson, the head of the Grand Trunk Railway, is now identified with this proposition for the first time, and it is proposed to make a deal between this new company and the government to settle the transportation problem in the North-west. I told the House some time ago that I did not think this was the right way to settle the transportation problem. I believe that the only way it can be solved is by the government ownership of the line that connects the main roads in Ontario with the main roads in the North-west, and my idea is to have a government-built and government-owned road from Port Arthur, or, if necessary from North Bay to Winnipeg. In that way the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Northern Railway would be at once put into the North-west. Imagine what would happen in the North-west to-morrow if this were carried out. What the Canadian Pacific Railway fear to-day most of all, and what I thought the government were trying to accomplish, was to put the Grand Trunk Railway into the North-west tomorrow. Under the proposition we have now before us, the Grand Trunk Railway will not be in the North-west for six years, even if they are there in ten years ; but by nationalizing one of the roads between the main systems of the east and the systems of the west, you can have the Grand Trunk Railway in the west toLmorrow. That is what the people of Canada want to see- they want to see the Grand Trunk Railway go into the North-west over a government-owned line, and over the same line they desire to see the people's railway, the Intercolonial Railway go. But we are told that the Canadian Pacific Railway have a special clause in their contract by which their rates are not to be interfered with until certain profits have been proved to have been made. The time came long ago when the cost of that road should have been investigated, and its rates brought under revision. But that has never been done, and I suppose it never will be done. But the way to regulate the Canadian Pacific Railway in regard to its rates and to give relief to the people of the North-west is to put the Grand Trunk Railway, the Canadian Northern Railway, and, above all, the Intercolonial Railway, in competition with it. That is a way that has been found satisfactory in regulating rates-to have one road owned and controlled by the government fixing the rates. Real competition will bring down rates regardless of special agreements. As I pointed out not long ago, in dealing with another question, the railway passenger fares in the state of New
York were settled by dealing with one railway. An Act was passed regulating rates on that one road, and while the other roads claimed that they had special privileges, yet, competition has compelled them to reduce their rates. So, the government could at once affect a reduction of the rates by proceeding in the right way. Negotiate with one of the big roads, or, if they will not negotiate, let the government build a new road and in that way give relief to the country. But I believe the building of a new road would not be a necessity. I believe the Canadian Pacific Railway or the Canadian Northern Railway would discuss this matter with the government and that the outcome of that discussion would be a determination to nationalize this railway through the country which Sir William Van Horne has called ' the spout.'
Now, what is a practical railway for the business that is to be done ? Clearly it is a high class road. The day has gone by for cheap railways. You must have ai high class railway; you must have a double track railway ; you must have a road without curves and without grades. With that, you will be able to carry wheat at the lowest possible rates, and so give the people relief. You can build as many one-liorse railways as you like, and they will do very little good in these days. We have built many of them, and built them with the people's money. But they do not solve the problem, for they are not in a position to carry freights at the lowest rates. My idea of a road to do that work is a road of the standard of the New York Central Railway, or better still, the Pennsylvania Railway. Such a road as that might cost $60,000 a mile or even more, but once built, it would carry immense trains at a very low cost, particularly in connection with our navigation system. I will go further, and say that the moment that line had been nationalized between Winnipeg and Lake Superior, I would go to the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway and would say :	Gentlemen, we
want the wheat of the North-west carried at the lowest possible rates not only over this government road from Winnipeg to Port Arthur, but over the roads in the east ; therefore, we will assist you to straighten out your roads from Midland or Owen Sound to Montreal or any other St. Lawrence port. Government assistance given in that way would bind the provinces together as nothing else will. But you will never solve the transportation problem by a one-horse railway through the wilds of New Brunswick, through the wilds of Quebec and through the wilds of Ontario. But you can solve it to-morrow by nationalizing the road between Winnipeg and Port Arthur, building it to the proper standard and then straightening out the roads in the east from the great lakes to the sea-board. It may be that these roads would be willing to be

nationalized between Midland and Montreal, or between Owen Sound and Montreal and Quebec. Probably the best line for a high class road would be from Midland connecting with the Canadian Pacific Railway system to Quebec, or it may be over the Canada Atlantic Railway, which could be taken over by the government and made a portion of the national system. These lines would be all run as complementary of our navigation system. We have spent immense sums in this country building up our ports and harbours and making our canals. The men who own and control the railways to-day are to a large extent the men opposed to transportation by water. A system of railways owned and controlled by the government, and not handed over immediately to a private corporation, should be the complement of our navigation system. That is a thing which has been left out of view in connection with transportation in this country. The only way in which our railways can be made the complement of our system of navigation is by the government controlling andi owning them. The proposition before the House does not begin to solve the question. All it is doing in the North-west is to give another one-horse railway to reach our prairie sections. It does not touch the vital issue at a single point. It is not going to reduce the transportation of grain a dollar in years to come. It is possible that negotiations may be going on to bring the Canadian Northern into this deal. I would like to see the Canadian Northern brought in this proposition to-day, and it may be brought in later on, but I would wish to see it brought in under the control of parliament and not of the Grand Trunk Railway. I am only indulging in guess work, but I am inclined to believe that the Canadian Northern Railway would be ready to make a deal of that kind. If we did that, it would grant immediate relief to the North-west. Is not that something worth striving for ?
I am told that government ownership is not a desirable thing. The right hon. gentleman made the confession here the other day-and I very much regretted to hear him make it-that because he stood once on the bleak shores of Georgian bay and saw ail the work which Mr. Booth had to perform to make traffic for his road, from that moment he lost faith in government ownership. Was there ever a more humiliating confession ? He did not give any study to the question; he did not inquire where government ownership had been tried; lie did not go into any details; but just because a fit of despondency came over him as he stood gazing around the bleak shores of Georgian bay, he made up his mind that government ownership was not a success. But had he inquired, he would have found that wherever tried it has been a success. It has solved the transportation problem Mr. MACLEAN.
in many countries. The people of England to-day are of opinion that government ownership must come there, because the transportation charges there are higher than anywhere else. The people of the United States are coming to the conviction that there must be a grand trunk railway between the east and the west owned and controlled by the federal authorities. With a road of that kind, all the other roads would be regulated by it. In Germany, Italy, Russia, Australia, Africa, government ownership has been tried and has succeeded. It is found to be the only system which gives the people satisfactory service at 'the lowest rates. Take the experience in Austro-Hungary. They have government railways in that country, administered by the government, and the constant aim of the government commissioners is to run the railways so as to give the lowest transportation rates, and you will find the lowest transportation rates for passengers there of any country of the world. If by government ownership you mean the kind of ownership we have in this country, I do not believe in it. The Intercolonial Raihvay, as it is administered, is not my ideal of government ownership. But if the Intercolonial Railway were taken out of politics, it would, if it were administered by commissioners independent of politics and members of parliament, do you mean to say that it would not make a better showing ? I would like to see a man like Sir Thos. Shaughnessey or Mr. Hays given control of our Intercolonial with instructions to run it in the interests of the people and keep it free from politics altogether. If that were done, it would give the best solution of the transportation prob-blem. Instead of building rivals to the Intercolonial Railway, keep it as it is, take it absolutely out of politics, put it under the administration of a man like Mr. Hays, and tell him to go ahead and extend it into the North-west and run it on such lines as to force every other company, the Canada Atlantic Railway, the Canadian Northern, the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway, to give the lowest possible rates. In that way relief would soon be accomplished.
You could nationalize a sufficient portion of our railways for my present purpose for a comparatively small sum. $20,000,000 will do it. But I do not believe that $100,000,000 will build the road proposed by the government.
How could you nationalize the three roads you have named for $20,000,000?
You could nationalize the road from Winnipeg to Port Arthur for $20,000,000 or less.

The hon. gentleman proposes to nationalize the Grand

Trunk Railway from Midland to Montreal, the Canadian Pacific Railway from Owien Sound to Montreal, the Canada Atlantic Railway and the Canadian Northern Railway from Port Arthur to Winnipeg-could all that be done for $20,000,000 ?
Very largely.
Those four roads?

If it is more than $20,000,000, what are we to think of the hon. gentleman's proposition, which he says would only cost $13,000,000, running from ocean to ocean? But the proposition submitted to the House, I submit, involves an expenditure of over a hundred millions. We are committing this country to a proposition involving an outlay of a hundred million dollars, and we are not to get anything for our money, but are immediately to give the road away to the Grand Trunk Railway. Thus we are not solving the problem but only buildidng a one-horse railway.
Is the Grand Trunk Railway a one-horse railway?

It will be from Moncton through the wilds of Quebec. No reason was given for it other than it would be a colonization road. The place to test government ownership and the building of a road by the government is the fat part and not the lean. Government ownership has been tried in this country always where it must fail. Politics have been mixied up with it, and it has been tried besides in an unproductive, bleak part of the country. But try it in the province of Ontario. What would the people of Ontario say to-day if the government came down with a proposition to parallel the Grand Trunk Railway and the Canadian Pacific Railway from Montreal to Toronto and to Niagara and the Detroit river and Georgian bay. That is a road which would furnish the key to the lock. The people of Ontario would like to see a hundred millions of their money spent in paralleling these roads in the province of Ontario, because such a road would run through the heart of the traffic and bring the other railways to time. That is what I would like. But I am now asking for a very modified form of government ownership, which would put the Grand Trunk Railway into the North-west to-morrow, which would give the Canadian Northern Railway an opportunity it has not now of developing and expanding in the Northwest, and above all, would bring the Intercolonial Railway into the North-west. The principle of government ownership is one which will find approval among the people. That is the kind of ownership which the people want and the kind of relief which the people of the North-west want. It would not cost a great deal and would solve the problem right away. The proposal now brought down does not involve government ownership, although we are asked to support it because it does. As soon as the road is constructed, the government will give it away. Why should we give these railways away? If we build them, why should we not own and control them and give every railway that desires it running powers over them by our leave, and not by the leave of the Grand Trunk Railway ? I want to see these railroads run over this new road, and have running privileges, but I wish the control of the road to be in the hands of the government, and not in the hands of the Grand Trunk Railway with power to discriminate against any outside road that may desire to use it.
There is another thing in respect of which I think the proposal involved in this Bill is an extraordinary one. I believe that in some way there are men associated with this scheme who hope to make money out of it in some way, who are seeking to take advantage of a large grant of public money in order to make fortunes for themselves. "Whether that is so or not, I cannot tell at the present time, we must wait and see. But my idea is that whatever money is spent on that road should be spent by the government in the interest of the people, and without any regard to the interest of private individuals who are seeking to make fortunes out of it. The history of railroad building in the past in connection with subsidies from parliament, irrespective of party, I make the broad statement, has been to build up the private fortunes of individuals. We don't want any more of that in this country; and yet I am afraid that in this bogus proposal which is said to involve the principle of government ownership, there may be a great deal of that. I want to see this road built by the people and owned by the people, in such a way that no private fortunes are made out of it, that no great grafts are to be worked, as we see they have been worked in the past. The suspicion is that they are being worked to-day, and that the project is brought forward in the interest of men who have had large experience in exploitations of various kinds. I do not know how much truth there is in that, and I am not going into it to-day. But in the light of the history of the past, all that should be avoided, and the people, for their money, should get a people's railway. They should get for their money a road that will bring relief to the people of the North-west to-morrow. The proposal of the government will only bring relief after ten years. The government should bring down a scheme that would put the Grand Trunk into the North-west to-morrow. I believe the Grand Trunk desire to get into the North-west to-morrow. I do not believe they desire ta build this line through Quebec, or through New Brunswick ; and I believe there is a clause in the Bill which says the Governor in Council may suspend

operations in connection with that if they see fit.
Now, what the Grand Trunk desire, I believe, is to get into the North-west at the . earliest possible moment; but certain parties, for reasons of one kind or another, are forcing the Grand Trunk to go through the bleak portions of Quebec and the Lauren-tian country, and through the wilds of New Brunswick. I do not believe the Grand Trunk themselves desire this proposal for one moment, but they do wish to devote all their energy to getting from North Bay, and as best they can, into the North-west and from there to the Pacific. I want to see the Grand Trunk get into the North-west, and the people of the North-west wish to see it there. But they wish to see it get there in the most desirable form. They do not wish to see it get there in this form, they do not [DOT]wish to see that great railroad tied up to the obligation of building a road, as is proposed, a road in Ontario, of building a road in Quebec, of building a road in New Brunswick. That won't solve the problem in the least, and it will take ten years to accomplish it. But the project suggested here today will solve it at once. What I suggest is that the whole energy of the Grand Trunk be devoted to getting to the Pacific. I believe in getting to the Orient by a new railway. I believe there is lots of traffic west of Winnipeg, lots of traffic through the Peace river country, lots of traffic in that district for a Canadian railway taking Canadian products to China and Japan. But the way to do that is to allow the Grand Trunk to devote its whole energy to getting to the west, not in building these roads at the present time to the north of us. They are not going to settle the transportation problem one bit; but building the road on the lines I have suggested will do it immediately, and will put the Grand Trunlo where I believe it wishes to be put-in the North-west to-morrow. As I said before, the Grand Trunk put in the North-west tomorrow, it may be over the Canadian Northern for the present, will be an immediate competitor of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and you will have the Canadian Pacific Railway changing its attitude and trying to serve the people of the North-west and cutting down rates. But as it is to-day, the whole energy of this parliament, and of the Grand Trunk, judging by the Bill as it now stands, are to be frittered away in building these roads through the wilderness of the eastern provinces.	.
Now, Mr. Chairman, later on I intend to discuss the question again, and to go perhaps more fully into it. But at present X only take the opportunity of entering a solemn protest on behalf of the people of Canada, and of the people of the North-west in particular, against this proposal. I do so because it does not give immediate relief to the North-west, it does not solve the problem, and it entails great expense upon the

country, and in every way is not in the public interest. I say now, in order that the Prime Minister may hear me, that what be should have done was to bring the great railroads into consultation, and say to them: We will nationalize our spout, we will allow you to run over it, we will let the Intercolonial run over it, we will make the Intercolonial a competitor of your road, we will fix the pace, and you must dance to that tune, if it is in the public interest. All that could have been done, all that could be done now. It could have been started five years ago. But all we are told is that the proposition to avail ourselves of this opportunity of government ownership is a mistake. I think it is no mistake. I think the one solution of the problem is government ownership, or at least government competition ; and on that line I enter this protest against the proposal. I think it is a wrong policy, I think it is a bad policy, I think it is against public interest, and it is not in the line of the progress that characterizes all other countries to-day in dealing with these great questions. Russia is building an immense railroad ; it may be primarily for national reasons, but it is also for transportation reasons. Australia is building up railroads all the time ; all the nations that have gone into public ownership are extending their systems, they are satisfied that they are right. We alone are going back on that principle. The right hon. gentleman, in this proposal, is going back on the principle of government ownership, because he proposes to denude in some way the Intercolonial. He is giving it a rival at its most important point, a Grand Trunk string to the Intrcolonial bow at very large cost and will effect but a small shortening of the distance. An hon. gentleman said the other day that he does not think it will save more than sixty miles. We have the Intercolonial to-day which is available ; it ought to be extended, it ought to be strengthened and improved ; it ought not to be run down by a competitor put alongside of it. It should be extended to the west through the province of Ontario. That would make it a great railroad, that would make it a people's railroad, then you would help the people of the North-west to solve the great transportation problem and give them immediate relief. By controlling the terminals you would control the whole situation. These terminals make the strength of a railroad's position. We are gradually spending immense sums on them. In that way you will bind the provinces together.
The right hon. gentleman, when he brought down his proposition the other day, said there was danger of the withdrawal of the bonding privilege. Is it not a fact to-day that we have an all-Canadian road from Halifax to Vancouver ? Suppose the Americans deprived us of the -bonding privilege to-morrow, we still have a Canadian railway in our own territory, controlled by this

parliament; and we will be no better able, when we have this new line of the government, than we are to-day to withstand any pressure that our neighbours may put upon us in connection with the bonding privilege.
So, that argument falls to the ground. We have an all-Canadian route to-day and we are spending $100,000,000-it may be $150,000,000-to get a road that will do nothing more as far as the bonding privileges are concerned than the roads we have today. As far as the sentimental reasons given are concerned, we will not have any better means of transportation than those existing by means of the roads we have now. They will bind the country together and the way to bind tfie country together is to reduce rates over these railways so as to give an opportunity to the community of exchanging their views and becoming acquainted with each other by means of travel. The people of the North-west Territories have to pay four cents a mile to travel on the railway and they cannot under those circumstances come east. The policy of the Canadian Pacific Railway is to take people into the North-west at one cent a mile and to charge them four cents a mile to bring them out again. That is not good public policy. In the province of Manitoba they have a three-cent a mile rate and railway competition made it. Probably the agreement that the Manitoba government made with the Canadian Northern may have had something to do with it. Governments are in a position to do different things to alleviate the grievances of the people in connection with transportation, but they must go the right way about it. In this case, the right way to go about it is not to devote ten years to the building of a new railway through the wilderness but to do something immediately right in the places where traffic is congested and right in the populous centres. There is one way to regulate traffic on railways and that is to regulate one road or to have a government-owned road in operation in competition with private-owned roads in the populous parts of the country because the effect of that competition will be to regulate traffic charges. The people of the North-west Territories not only want a reduction in the traffic charges, but they want increased accommodation for moving their freight. They say they have a congested state of affairs up there. They never can get rid of that congestion of traffic by the adoption of the proposal of the government which is now before us because there can be no solving of the problem by the building of a road through the wilderness. If the government study the question they will see that their proposition is not feasible, they will withdraw from their present position and they will begin to negotiate with the Canadian Pacific Railway and with the Canadian Northern Railway, and if they do negotiate and do get possession of a road do not let them give it away the 246
moment they get it, but get it for the people and keep it because it will have a regulative influence upon all the roads. If these-negotiations are going on, as I believe thejr are going on with Sir Charles Rivers-Wil-son, they ought to be absolutely based upon the principle of government ownership of the Canadian Northern Railway, and if we have that we will have the Grand Trunk Pacific in the west to-morrow, we will have 1,700 miles of railway competing with the Canadian Pacific Railway and we will have the resources of that great road extending its line across the plains and getting to the Pacific ocean, and in securing that we will be doing something for the people of this country. That is the issue between my idea and the idea submitted by the government. I believe my idea is one that will meet with the sanction of the people. It is an idea that I have been following very closely. I have been studying the question, I have been listening to men from all portions of the country, I have been reading the press, and if there is one thing to-day in the public mind more conspicuous than another, it is that the solution of the transportation problem whether by railways or waterways, is from the adoption of the principle of government owership, the building up of one system of railways and making the rates on this system as they ought to be so that other roads operating in competition with this government road will have to come down to these rates and give equal treatment and facilities to the people. Mr. Chairman, I beg to withdraw the motion.
Motion (Mr. Maclean) withdrawn, and section as amended agreed to.
On section 4,
That section four be reconsidered for the purpose of amending it by substituting the word ' forty ' for the word * seventy ' in the first line.

This is, I suppose, in view of the proposition that the company shall build only from Winnipeg to the Pacific ocean. What will the length of the line be ?
Mr. McCarthy. Between 1,600 and 1,800 miles.

This will give a capitalization of how much per mile ?
Mr. McCarthy. A little less than $30,000 per mile-$27,000 or $28,000 per mile.
What is the estimate of the cost of these 1,600 or 1,800 miles ?

My information is that the cost will be $20,000 per mile on the



prairie section, and $50,000 per mile on tlie mountain section.
This will Include rolling stock 1

My information is that in addition to that there will be about $7,000 per mile for rolling stock, so that the cost will be $27,000 per mile on the prairie section, and $57,000 per mile on the mountain section.
What does that include in the shape of rolling stock ?
My information does not go as far as that.

We were informed that the cost for the prairie section would be very much less than the hon. gentleman
states when we were' discussing another matter this session. Is that estimate based upon any reports of engineers ?

I cannot say as to that, but I can say this that the railway to which the hon. gentleman referred has only built a 56 pound rail, and the intention of this railway is to build an SO pound rail which will make a very great difference. The cost of a standard railway will be much higher. The requirements of the contract are that as far as practicable the railway is to be built to equal the line of the Grand Trunk Railway between Montreal and Toronto.
What is the weight of that rail ?
Eighty pounds, I understand.
What will be the location of the railway between Winnipeg and Edmonton ?

It is set out in section 12, of the Bill.
To a 'point at or near the city of Winnipeg ; thence westerly and north-westerly, passing through or near Battleford, Edmonton and Dun-vegan, or by such other more feasible route as is hereafter located, but following in a general direction that herein indicated, and by way of either the Peace River Pass or the Pine River Pass.
There is another clause which requires the line to be located in a specific way, and, of course, it is subject to the approval of the Governor in Council.
Will the proposed line run north or south of the proposed Canadian Northern Railway line V

North, I understand ; but, of course, that is not settled. The committee spent several days considering the question as between the three railways, and finally a clause was added that at no point they are to be closer than 30 miles. I Mr. McCarthy.	.

Does the hon. gentleman (Mr. McCarthy) mean to say that this road is going to run north of the Canadian Northern Railway to any extent after it passes Winnipeg ?
Mr. McCarthy. I cannot say.

As outlined on the map, if that is any guide, it runs between the Manitoba and the north-west branch of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and the main line of the Canadian Pacific Railway, and the Canadian Northern Railway runs far north of the Manitoba and north-western branch. After it passes Portage la Prairie at any rate it surely must run south, and very far south of the Canadian Northern Railway.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Roche) knows the country very much better than I do, and, it would be idle for me to state where the railroad is going to run. The ordinary observances have been followed in this charter, stating that it shall start from a point at or near a certain place, and then run to a certain other point. This charter is subject to more restrictions than other charters in respect to this 30-mile limit ; it is subject to the general provisions of the Railway Act, and it is also subject to the Governor in Council deeming its location reasonable. Until it is absolutely located, one cannot speak definitely as to whether it will be north or south of either ohe or the other line.

If it runs south of the Canadian Northern Railway it ought to be a much cheaper road to construct than the Canadian Northern Railway. When I took exception to the estimate of $19,000 per mile for the Canadian Northern Railway, the reason given for the high estimate was that it included several expensive bridges. If $19,000 was sufficient for the Canadian Northern Railway, including bridges, this road going considerably south would be an easier road to construct, and yet we have an estimate of $27,000 per mile, including $7,000 for equipment. I think that estimate was exaggerated.
Mr. McCarthy. The hon. gentleman knows that I am not going to construct the road, and that I am merely giving the information which I have. Let me call attention to the fact that parliament is only guaranteeing on the prairie section a maximum of $13,000 per mile. If seventy-five per cent of the cost is less than that, then the guarantee is only up to seventy-five per cent. Whatever it costs will be ascertained and be subject to the control of the Governor in Council.

Does the hon. gentleman mean to intimate that it is no concern of this House what this road shall be capitalized at ? Surely it is Important to the

people of tlie country whom we are supposed to represent to know whether it shall be capitalized at a larger amount than is necessary to build the road, because they would be entitled to charge rates according to the amount of their capitalization. It is, therefore, important to know this. The hon. member (Mr. Roche) has said tha(, this road which is going to go south of the Canadian Northern Railway would be a much easier road to build, and it seems to me that $20,000 per mile is a larger capitalization than should be allowed. That with $7,000 a mile for rolling stock is simply absurd.

With respect to the amount stated for rolling stock, I may say that when the contract was about to be entered into with the railway company, it was thought advisable to have the opinion of Mr. Schreiber, chief engineer of government railways, and he told us that a proper equipment for such a railway would amount to $6,000 or $7,000 a mile. We, therefore, give my hon. friend the expert opinion of a man who is qualified to speak on the subject.
Is it in writing?

I have no doubt that we can get it in writing. It was given to the acting Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Fielding) in my presence. I am not sure whether he asked it in writing, but I will ask for a certificate from Mr. Schreiber.

The estimated length from Edmonton to the coast is about 1,000 miles, and the length from Winnipeg to Edmonton 000 or 700 miles, making 1,700 miles in all. Why does the Minister of Justice require that the first equipment of rolling stock shall the $15,000,000, apportioned to the western section ?

We estimated the length of the road and multiplying it by seven, it came to $18,300,000 and we put it down at $20,000,000, and the company agreed. Of course, if my hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Haggart) wishes to set up his opinion against that of Mr. Schreiber he is perfectly free to do so, but we took the opinion of a. man, who in our judgment, is competent to advise.
I am not talking about my opinion at all, but I say that 700 miles at $7,000 per mile would not be $15,000,000. '
It would be $11,900,000 on those figures.

The government saw that the estimate would be more than
sufficient, but they only apportioned $5,000.000 of it for the whole line from Winnipeg to Quebec. *	.
That is in the Bill.

The hon. gentleman has not read the contract. The $5,000,000 with respect to the eastern end is especially apportioned for the purpose of being security to us for the operation of the road. That is to say, of the $20,000,000 for rolling stock, we ear-mark $5,000,000, apportion that to the eastern end and hold that as a special guarantee. That does not mean that the $5,000,000 is the extent of the equipment ; it is the extent of the guarantee.
But the whole stock of the road is security for the running of the road.

For the first issue of bonds the whole stock is security on the western end, but with respect to the eastern end, we have to take a special security, because in that case they are only our tenants, and we ear-mark $5,000,000 of that stock which is to be apportioned to the eastern end, and will be security to us for the due performance of all the work.
Mi-. CLARKE. Do you get a first or second mortgage on that ?

We get a first mortgage. We first take security on the whole $20,000,000 on our guarantee, and with respect to the $5,000,000 in addition to the fact that it is a security to us for the guarantee of the bonds at the western end, we take it as a special security In connection with the eastern end.

There seems to be a considerable lack of information as to the location of the line west of Winnipeg. Is that indefiniteness due to the fact that negotiations are going on for the acquirement of the Canadian Northern system by the new company ?

Not at all. It is simply due to the fact that we are observing with reference to this railway enterprise all the rules that we observe with reference to other companies which come before us for charters. When a charter is granted to a railway company, it comes under the operation of the general Railway Act, which provides that all maps, plans, and profiles of the road shall be submitted for the approval of the Railway Committee of the Privy Council; and here special provision is made for the location of the western end, which is to be subject to the approval of the government.

I am informed that it is impossible for this company to comply with the condition that the line running westerly and northerly from Winnipeg to Edmonton shall keep 30 or 40 miles from any other line. I want to ask if negotiations are going on between this company and the

Canadian Northern ? If so, we can understand why there is such indefiniteness in the Bill. If this company acquired the Canadian Northern, it would not be paralleling its lines.

My hon. friend must not be too inquisitive, and ask us to tell him what negotiations are going on between two railway companies. As to what may be going on between the Grand Trunk Company and the Canadian Northern, we know nothing. It is not to our knowledge that any such negotiations are going on. We assume that such an important corporation would not undertake to build a railway through a country where they could not locate it.
I am given to understand by those acquainted with the country that it is physically impossible to build this railway 40 miles north of the Canadian Northern Railway.
I am sure that the railway company will be impressed with this discussion. The Grand Trunk Railway Company have a knowledge of the country because they have surveyors there now locating the line.
We have the assurance from one high authority that no survey has yet been made.
Surveys have been going on for the past six months.
Has the right hon. gentleman any information with reference to the passes ? The company has power under the Bill to take the Peace river or the Pine river pass, and to go to any port on the Pacific.
They have to go to Port Simpson.
If that is so, that virtually locates the line. The Bill says at or near Port Simpson or Bute Inlet or any other port on the Pacific.

The intention certainly is to go to Port Simpson unless very cogent reasons are brought to the contrary. There is no doubt whatever, from the explorations we have had, that Port Simpson is decidedly the best harbour we have in British Columbia.
I think so myself.

When this Grand Trunk Pacific Bill was before the Railway Committee. several hon. gentlemen refrained from discussing the merits of this railway on the promise of the Minister of Finance, acting Minister of Railways and Canals, that when the government scheme for as-Mr. CLARKE.
sisting the Grand Trunk Pacific should be submitted to parliament, the government would be in a position to state definitely what the route would be. That was the pledge given to the Railway Committee by the hon. gentleman.
Not at all.
I pledge my word of honour that that pledge was given, and if It Is not carried out now, it only shows that we cannot rely on a pledge when it is given.

It seems to me, taking this clause in connection with clause 13, that the capitalization of the company is pretty large-in fact, very excessive. Under section 13 you have $20,000 per mile of bonds authorized on the prairie section and $50,000 on the mountain section ; and you have, under section 4, $45,000,000 of capital authorized for a road between 1,600 and 1,800 miles in length. Has my hon. friend who is moving the Bill made any estimate of 'wlnit the total capitalization would amount to ?

My hon. friend will remember that we discussed this fully before the committee before. I am unable to apply the term capital in the way he does. I cannot understand the bonding privilege as capital. A bonding privilege is something that may be executed to its fullest extent, or it may not be. I have therefore made no calculation, and am unable to answer the hon. gentleman's question.

I would suppose that capital, in the sense in which I am using it, would include the expenditure of .money raised by bonds as well as the ex-'penditure of money raised by the issue of capital stock. This railway might be built altogether, as many other railways are, with the money raised from the sale of the bonds. Suppose the common stock of this company were $50,000, and it were given bonding power sufficient to build the whole road ; would not the question of capital in that case be involved in the amount of the bond issue ? It is none the less involved because you fix a substantial sum as the capital stock of the company. The result will be that you will have this company capitalized, including the bond issue, to the extent of some $57,000 per mile, and my hon. friend does not pretend that the road on the prairie, including equipment, will cost more than $27,000 per mile. I am still of opinion, notwithstanding what has been said to the contrary, that a capitalization of that kind may interfere to a great extent with the control of the rates hereafter. It is impossible, looking at the conditions as they are, to say that the amount of outstanding bonds and capital stock in the hands of bona fide holders will not affect the question of the control of rates in thei future. These mat-

ters will be looked at by the tribunal, whatever it may be, which has to deal with the question of control of rates in the future.
I may say further that it is remarkable we have not a more definite statement as to where the location will be. The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche) has said that it will be very much cheaper if built south of the proposed line of the Canadian Northern Railway than if built thirty miles north. But the promoter of the Bill is unable to say whether or not this company proposes to build north or south of the Canadian Northern Railway. I should think that some member of the government should be prepared to make an announcement on that point, in view of the fact that the government has introduced a measure which contemplates assistance to this company of a very substantial amount, not only on the mountain, but the prairie section as well. Surely the government takes some interest in this question of capitalization. It is a question of practical interest to everybody throughout the country. The people believe that a high capitalization will materially interfere with that control of the rates which is desirable we should have. The information of my hon. friend is extremely indefinite and based on such insufficient data that we are not very much inclined to accept his estimate of the cost of the road across the prairie section. We have no information before the House in the shape of engineers' estimates that I am aware of, and we know that railways have been built on the prairie section for very much less than the hon. gentleman suggests. It is quite true that the standard of this road may be somewhat higher, but we are merely guessing unless we have some information of the kind to which I have referred. Why should this road have a capitalization of $57,000 per mile ?
That is on the mountain section.

No, I am speaking of the whole road. On the mountain section, you have not only the capitalization included in the stock issue, but a possible capitalization of $50,000 per mile of a bond issue as well. We have no exact information as to the length of the mountain and the prairie section. We may presume that the prairie section will be 1,100 long and the mountain section 000. That is the nearest approach we can make to it, from the somewhat indefinite statement made by my hon. friend in charge of the Bill. '

It seems to me that the promoter of the Bill should give some reasons why he is making this reduction. What is the basis upon which he is working ? The original Bill required a capital of $75,000,000. He has struck off $30,000,000 and made the capital $45,000,000. According to the position presented by the First Minister, the company are to be rid of the building of the road from Winnipeg to Moncton. This would be the more expensive part of the line. Under the first arrangement, they were to build from Moncton to the coast. 'They are getting rid of the more expensive portion and yet their capital is allowed to remain at considerable more than half the original amount. This committee should have the basis on which the hon. gentleman makes his deduction. The hon. gentleman declines to answer. That is just what I expected. Thefe is evidently no basis. They have simply lumped the matter just as they did the whole transaction. They have gone into it without any information. The very gentleman who promoted this Bill before the Railway Committee and who has been lauded as such a railway builder, did not actually know anything about the country. He did not know where Lake Nepigon was ; lie did not know the length of the line and the nature of the country, and was simply taking a leap in the dark. We need not ask for definite information, for we are not given even indefinite information. But it seems to me that when the government is going to give such substantial assistance to the enterprise, these men who are promoting the Bill should have the information we are asking for.

The committee lias already had a good deal of information. It is provided in the contract that the mining section is to be assisted by the guarantee of the government to the extent of 75 per cent on its cost, and the liability of the government is in no case to exceed $30,000 per mile in that section. It is assumed that the mountain section is between GOO and 700 miles in length. It is not possible to say exactly, but it will not be less than GOO or more than 700. Suppose it is 600. The bonds to be guaranteed by the government to the extent of 75 per cent will cover an amount of $18,000,000. The other twenty-five per cent will bring the amount to $24,000,000. This is a very low estimate, but that would be the lowest cost of the mountain section. It is estimated that the prairie section will be between 1,000 and 1,100 miles long. On that section we guarantee that bonds of the company to the extent of 75 per cent of the cost, our liability not to exceed $13,000 per mile. As to that we have some data, because some time ago we had a Bill passed in this House under somewhat similar circumstances over the same prairie section, in which it was agreed that we shoull guarantee the bonds of that body. It seemed a fair arrangement, and therefore, taking the cost of that part of the road at $13,000,000, as regards the government guarantee, you will have the whole cost of the prairie section between $16,000,000 and $17,000,000. Add $25,000,000 for the mountain section and you will have a total

cost of $42,000,000. Then you must add $20,000,000 of rolling stock, which brings the amount to $62,000,000. My hon. friend knows well that the stock to be issued by the company is an unknown quantity, as regards the amount which it will realize. As my hon. friend knows, it would not realize one hundred cents on the dollar, but only what the confidence of the people aud the state of the market may fix. Under these circumstances, the company must have some leeway. In all cases in building a railway like this, you must give power to issue bonds and stock to a certain extent above the par value. If you knew that you were going to get exactly the face value of these securities you could calculate in that way what you would require. But you are not able to do so, consequently you must fix a wider limit.

The bonds are not counted in the capital stock. You must have capital to cover the margin between the seventy-five per cent guaranteed by the government and the cost of the road. On the mountain section there will be $6,000,000 and on the prairie section about the same-at any rate a total of $11,000,000 or $12,000,000 as I remember it. But, if you require $12,000,000 to make up the difference between what will be realized from the sale of the bonds guaranteed by the government and the actual cost of the road, what is the need of this capitalization of $45,000,000 ? It seems to me, that the public would have more confidence in this enterprise and also would give a higher price for the stock if the authorized issue was not so large. For, if $45,000,000 of stock is issued, as this will not increase the earnings, you have that much less security for a good return to the persons who invest. Then we must consider the people who are to be served by the line. There can be no possible question that that is a matter that will be taken into consideration when the tariff of tolls is to be fixed for this road by the Railway Commission under the Act now before parliament. The question will be asked :	What is the
capital of the road ; what interest must be paid to those who have invested their money in the enterprise ? For that reason it is very important that we should know somewhat accurately the basis on which this calculation has been made up. If it is reasonable that a capital of $45,000,000 should be allowed, this committee will cheerfully grant it. But, until the information is before it, the committee ought not to be asked to authorize such a capitalization as is here proposed.

Further than that, the right hon. gentleman has dealt only with the bonds guaranteed by the government. But that does not touch the question I was dealing with, the amount of bonds and capital stock the company is allowed to issue-$50,000 of bonds per mile Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
on the mountain section and $20,000 of bonds per mile on the prairie section. Let us see, taking the estimates given by the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. McCarthy), what the road is to cost. He says it will cost $20,000 a mile for the prairie section. That, I believe is excessive. Then, he asks $7,000 a mile for rolling stock which is also pretty liberal. That makes $27,000 a mile for the prairie section of say 1,100 miles, or a total of $29,700,000. Then take the mountain section. It is said that this would cost $50,000 a mile, add $7,000 for the rolling stock and you have $57,000 a mile, for say 600 miles, or a total of $34,200,000. Sb, the cost of the whole road, even on these pretty liberal estimates would be $63,900,000. How do you propose to capitalize the company in view of that ? In the first place you give $45,000,000 of stock, and bonding powers amounting to $52,000,000, or a total capitalization of $97,000,000, which is $33,000,000 more than the whole cost of the road, even according to the very liberal estimates of the hon. member for North Simcoe. It may be true, as the right hon. Prime Minister (Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) has said, that you must give some leeway. But what excuse is there for a leeway of $33,000,000 on a total estimated cost of $63,900,000 ? What excuse is there for that ? Does the right hon. gentleman pretend to say that that very extravagant capitalization, when the securities have been sold and have passed into the hands of bona fide purchasers, will not exercise an influence upon the control of rates upon that ? I believe it is bound to exercise a very considerable influence, and I protest for my part, against this excess of $33,000,000 over the very liberal estimates submitted to the House by the hon. gentleman who is promoting the Bill.

I would like to ask the right hon. First Minister whether, as a matter of fact, it is not the intention of the parties to these negotiations that the Grand Trunk Railway Company-not the Grand Trunk Pacific, but the Grand Trunk-shall receive a present of $25,000,000 of this stock? Under the 27th section of the agreement between the government and the Grand Trunk Pacific, it is provided that the Grand Trunk Railway Company shall acquire and take $25,000,000 of the stock, and shall also hold it during fifty years. It strikes me that the Grand Trunk Railway Company would find it rather difficult to raise $25,000,000 to pay for that stock, unless they could afterwards sell the stock, and under the contract this is just what they cannot do, for they must hold it. I doubt whether there is any intention as between the two companies, the Grand Trunk and the Grand Trunk Pacific, that the Grand Trunk shall pay a dollar on that stock. I think it will turn out that this stock is to be given as a recompense to the Grand Trunk for guaranteeing 25 per cent

of the cost of the road. They will get that for their guarantee, while the country will get nothing.
Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. Barker) point out in this Bill where there would be any authority for the Grand Trunk Pacific to do what he suggests V

I only read from the section of the contract which says :
The company undertakes

That is,.the Grand Trunk Pacific Company undertakes, for the Grand Trunk undertakes nothing

-.that the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada shall acquire and take the said common stock to the amount of twenty-five million dollars, except shares held by directors not exceeding one thousand shares, and shall hold the shares during the term of the said lease, and so long as any of the bonds guaranteed by the government under the terms of this agreement shall remain outstanding and unpaid.
Looking at that from a common sense standpoint and in view of the fact that it is much to be doubted whether the Grand Trunk Company could afford to pay $25,000,000 for that stock-I do not suppose the Grand Trunk Pacific expect the Grand Trunk Railway Company shareholders to acquire so much stock and remain liable to be called upon to pay one hundred cents on the dollar-I infer that there will be what is commonly known as a dicker, and the money advanced on the bonds will be apparently advanced on the stock. By some of the ways unknown to dealers in stock the Grand Trunk Railway Company will get the stock without any liability ; there will be, as I said, simply a present made to the Grand Trunk of $25,000,000 out of this $45,000,000 of stock.
