There is no limit to assumptions, except the imagination of the gentleman who makes them. But I would repeat my question and ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Barker) to point out where the Grand Trunk Pacific would have the authority to make sucli a ' dicker' as he speaks of.

I would like to ask a question that I was about to ask when the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) rose, and that is, what the government proposes that the Grand Trunk shall pay for the $25,000,000 of stock that they are supposed to acquire. If the Grand Trunk is coming into this thing, it should show its good faith. We ought to have some assurance that, if that company acquires $25,000,000 of stock, it will pay for it. If it pays for it, this country will be relieved to that extent of the actual cost of the road.

Irishmanlike, my hon. friend answers one question by asking another. I would like the hon.
member for Hamilton (Mr. Barker) to answer the question I put.

The minister has heard of the various methods that have been adopted in the past in ordinary commercial companies, and In what are called industrial companies, by which an immense amount of stock is placed upon the market as paid-up stock when not a dollar Is paid upon it. There are various ways of doing it. We know that there have been large manufacturing concerns in which a million or two millions of stock have been issued as paid-up stock and never a dollar has been paid upon it, and yet it has gone out to the public, and the public have bought it as paid-up stock, and to all intents and purposes, it is so far as legal obligation goes, paid-up stock.

The Joint Stock Companies Act is known to us, the Railway Act is known to us all, and 1 would like the hon. gentleman to point out in the Joint Stock Companies Act or in the Railway Act anything that will justify the statement he has made.
-Does the hon. gentleman mean seriously to assure this House that under this contract if the Grand Trunk Railway take twenty-five millions of that stock, they are going to pay for it ?
I am not here to say what I think, I am here for the purpose of applying the law. The hon. gentleman has made a statement, and 1 want him to point out by what law he justifies that statement.
Why can it not he done under section 11 ? 'The question has already been asked.
I press for an answer to iny question.
I would like my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) to point out any section of any law that justifies his statement.

I know this, that bonds can be sold for what they are worth, and tlie Grand Trunk Railway Company can take stock at one hundred cents on the dollar and take bonds at five cents on the dollar, and buy both. The hon. gentleman has heard of such a transaction.
As to bonds, yes ; as to stock, no.

Very well, if some people in the same transaction want to buy both bonds and stock, they can buy very little in bonds and a great deal In stock. Very much like the old well-known practice under the Duncan Act, where a man paid five cents for a bit of ginger bread and got whiskey free.

I do not think we have any law in this country which says that those who subscribe for stock must pay for it.
Mr. MAC-LEAN. What are the Grand Trunk Railway to pay for this $25,000,000 of stock?
So far as I am concerned, under the law, they have got to pay full value for it.
As a member of the administration, has he made a contract with this road, or does he know that they intend to pay the cash ?
I know what the law requires of them, and I expect them to comply with the law.

Here is a contract involving $25,000,000, and we have no assurance from the government whether this $25,000,000 is to be in money, or whether it is to be practically a gift to the Grand Trunk Railway.
At six o'clock, committee took recess.
After Recess.
Committee resumed at eight o'clock.
On section 4,

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the amendment be adopted?

We were to have had some explanation about that. We would like the promoter of the Bill or some one representing the government to tell us what is to be done with this twenty-five million dollars worth of stock that the Grand Trunk Railway Company are to take up, when they are acquiring it what they are to give for it. and if the money that they give for it is to be devoted to the purpose of constructing the road. If that is the case it alters very largely the financial aspect of the proposition. Before the committee rose at six o'clock, when that question was up, we were expecting some information on that point either from the .government or the promoter of the Bill. I ask again for that information.

I cannot understand the difficulty that my hon. friend (Mr. Maclean) sees in the matter. There is no difference in this Bill from any other Bill respecting capital stock, and I am at a loss to understand how you can mix the privilege of issuing bonds and debentures with capital stock. The issue of bond or debenture requires the placing of the assets of the company of a mortgage, and that mortgage must be paid off in this case within fifty years. If that mortgage is paid off. the company are relieved of their obligation, but if it is not paid off. then the mortgagees have the right to foreclose the Mr. BARKER.
mortgage on the road. How you can mix up with capital the placing of a mortgage on the assets is more than I can understand. This is capital stock to be issued for ordinary purposes. It is not an exorbitant sum. It is greatly reduced as compared with the Canadian -Pacific Railway or any other railway company that ever asked for corporate powers from this parliament, and upon this clause I cannot see how you can mix up the capital stock with the bonding privilege. This is a fair capitalization. I have not heard any criticism of the amount of the capitalization except by joining it with the bonding privilege. I cannot understand the view which hon. gentlemen take, because every bond issued is secured by a mortgage. On onie side of the ledger you have the assets, on the other side you have the mortgage, and you cannot make the capital any better or any worse because one balances the other.

I do not think that tiny one desires to mix up the capital stock of this company and the bonds except the promoter himself, and it appears to me from what lie has said now and said before, that he is rather desirous of confusing our minds upon this question. The stock of the company, we are told, is to he $45,000,000. and of that $25,000,000 is to lie acquired by the Grand Trunk Railway Company. What we want to know is what becomes of this $25,000,000 after it is acquired by the Grand Trunk Railway Company?
They have to hold it.

Is it intended that they receive that as a gift for promoting this gigantic scheme? Is it intended that that $25,000,000 is to be divided amongst the provisional directors as their compensation for promoting this gigantic undertaking ? Is it intended that they shall purchase it, and if so, at what price shall they receive it-25 cents on the dollar or 50 cents on the dollar, or will they get par for it ? I am very suspicious that this $25,000,000 is to go to the Grand Trunk Railway Company to be divided amongst the directors as compensation for promoting this scheme. There is certainly something mysterious about it from the peculiar wording of the resolution and from the peculiar manner in which the promoter has endeavoured to answer the questions that have been propounded from this side of the House. I think we must have some specific declaration as to what will ultimately become of that $25,000,000, whether tile par value of the stock is to be realized from the Grand Trunk Railway Company and whether the $25,000,000 goes into the construction of this road.

I am rather surprised that my hon. friend (Mr. Henderson), if he has read the contract,

should make that statement. I think we have a right to assume that if the Grand Trunk Railway Company subscribe for this stock they will carry out their agreement according to law. It will be fraudulent to subscribe for this stock in some roundabout way, and to obtain it in a manner not in accordance with the laws of the country. My hon. friend suggested that they might dispose of this stock to some other parties. It is clearly agreed that they are to hold this stock as the Grand Trunk Railway Company, and they cannot dispose of it. Having entered into an agreement with the parliament of Canada to hold the stock, it would be a violation of the whole agreement should they attempt to dispose of it.
I suppose they would be liable to all the penalties that would be incurred for a breach of contract. There might even be a foreclosure of the mortgage. I do not think there is anything but what appears to be a straight business contract according to the laws of the country, and we have every reason to assume that a large and responsible company such as the Grand Trunk Railway Company would carry out any agreement that they entered into. I would be very sorry to think that there was anything in the Bill or the contract that would appear to be otherwise.

Is it the intention that the Grand Trunk Railway Company in taking up this $25,000,000 of stock shall practically furnish $25,000,000 towards this undertaking? If that is the intention it would appear to be a bona fide transaction, but I confess from the manner in which the promoter answered the questions on this point it led to a great deal of doubt in my mind as to whether this was the intention or not.

Has the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Henderson) any idea that if the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company were to be wound up, the shareholders of that company would not have to pay 100 cents on the dollar, and if lie has not any doubt upon that point he cannot have any doubt upon the question he is asking. When he endeavours to charge me with mixing up the bonding privileges and the capital stock. I absolutely repudiate his statement. I did not mix them up. The hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) and other lion, gentlemen on the other side of the House, when the discussion was up here the other day. sought to add the capital stock and bonding privileges together, to divide the mileage of the road into that and to show that this road was capitalized by the result per mile. That is absolutely foundationless. The premises are not correct. A bond that is issued cannot he said to be part of the capital stock of any kind of a company, because every bond is secured by mortgage. You have the assets upon one side and the
bonds upon the other, and if the bonds are not liaid the right of foreclosure can be exercised in this case at the end of fifty years. This is the ordinary case of a company asking for incorporation. When a railway company comes here asking- for incorporation, it has its capital stock and it has its bonding privileges. We have never heard of this discussion before. We have never heard of the process of adding bonding privileges and capital stock together and saying that the capitalization of the company is the result of that addition. I do not think, in business parlance, that that is a correct way of stating the case. I think it is absolutely incorrect, and the question is whether $45,000,000 is a fair capitalization for the company or whether it is not. The Canadian Pacific Railway, which will possibly have twice as _ much mileage as this road, have a capitalization of $85,000,000. In addition to that they received $25,000,000 in cash, $35,000,000 of railway constructed, and 25,000.000_ acres in land. I am not charging that the aid which was given to the Canadian Pacific Railway was improperly given, but when you put the two cases in parallel columns, it cannot be I argued that the capitalization of this company is unfair or that it is inadequate to the requirements of the company. The bonds must be met in fifty years and it is not fair to mix capital stock with bonding privileges.

I do not think this Bill is to be considered as an ordinary Bill going through the House under the same circumstances as most Bills, and I think my hon. friend (Mr. McCarthy) does not quite seize the sense of the argument on this side of the House as regards capitalization. The object of this great enterprise is to reduce rates, and that consideration was given- to the bonded indebtedness of the company, and the argument founded upon that was that the capital should not be made too large, because, if the bonded indebtedness represented a very large sum requiring payment of interest and it was necessary to pay interest upon an exorbitant amount of capital stock, the real object of all our efforts would not be attained ; that is to say, the payment of interest upon the bonded indebtedness and the payment of dividends upon the stock would prevent our attaining a great reduction of the rates. That is the way I understood the argument. As to an enterprise of this kind having a great effect on the reduction of rates, experience has proved the contrary ; experience has proved that when there are rival companies rates are not reduced. There is increased accommodation, greater conveniences and more comfort, but ail arrangement is generally arrived at between rival lines so as not to reduce the rates, at all events to such a degree as that provision will not be made for the payment of interest on the bonds

and also for doing justice to the shareholders of the stock of the company. It is therefore very natural to say that the bonded indebtedness being so much per mile and there being a second mortgage authorized, you will find that if you have a capital of $45,000,000 you will not be able to give to the western people that reduction of rates which they have a right to expect. I have an open mind on the question whether it will not be necessary for the company to have a capital of $45,000,000. I take it that the company will have to expend, over and above the bonds which it is authorized to issue, a sum approximating $10,000 per mile for the mountain section, because the report of the engineers made in 1877 for the route which the company has chosen to Bute Inlet represents an expenditure of $60,000 per mile, covering 523 miles. The authorized bonding in that region is only $50,000 per mile, so that the company will have to spend $10,000 per mile at least, if we are to have the standard railway that is stipulated in the contract, without taking into consideration the terminal facilities which the company is obliged to provide at Fort Simpson. In addition to that, the amendments which have been adopted to-day authorize the company to build branch lines to North Bay, to Montreal, to Port Arthur, and also tramways each not exceeding ten miles in length in British Columbia. I doubt very much if the company will be able to give us a line of railway in the prairie section of the standard required by the agreement for $20,000 per mile. [DOT] It may be so, but there are a great many rivers there and one or two watersheds, and the land is not absolutely flat. For my own part, I have an open mind on the question of the $45,000,000 capitalization. My hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker) has raised a question of very great importance, and one which was probably suggested by the latitude found in section 11 of the Bill. He asked for distinct information as to whether the Grand Trunk Railway is going to put into this company cash or its absolute equivalent to the amount of $25,000,000. That is a very important question, because the agreement made with the company, and which was emphasized by the Prime Minister, requires the company to put $25,000,000 into the enterprise, If the company is to get $25,000,000 in any other way ; if it is to get it in the way of a gratuity for promoting the Bill, or if it is in any way permitted to not carry out what seems to be the letter and spirit of the agreement, then it is a very important matter upon which we should be fully enlightened.

There is a feature of this discussion which is somewhat novel. Gentlemen on the other side contend that freight rates are fixed in consideration of the amount of capital in the way of stock or bonds that is put on the market. I would Mr. MONK.
j ask these gentlemen opposite, if any one of them has ever had anything to to do with the fixing of rates upon railways, and if so can he tell of one solitary case where the capital stock or the bonds that were issued entered into that consideration in the slightest degree. I submit that the fixing of rates on railways is determined upon a different basis altogether. It seems to me that we would be mere children to suppose that the tribunal which has the fixing of the rates j would take into consideration, not the dollars and cents that the road costs actually in money, but the amount of stock and j bonds that have been put upon the market. I make bold to say that no such considera-J tion has ever prevailed yet in the fixing of j rates upon a railway.
I think a great many ex-j amples might be given.
Can the hon. gentleman I give me one case in which it has been done?
It is certainly an important element in determining the rates on a rail-| way like this.
Can you give me a single case ?

There are many cases which might be mentioned in the United States, but without going further than Montreal, I might say that in the case of the Montreal Street Railway that was an element in determining its rates. It was alleged by the Montreal Street Railway Company-that their rates could not he made lower and a reasonable dividend paid to the holders of stock, and so the amount of the stock was taken into consideration. Also, in the case of the Montreal Light, Heat and Power Company, it was urged that the rates could not be made lower on account of the large capitalization |of the company, which. I think, is $17,000,000. It is a question frequently raised on behalf of the company when a company is called upon to reduce its rates.

I do not see wherein the statement of the hon. gentleman has the slightest bearing on the case we are discussing. I repeat my statement, that I do not believe a solitary case can be cited in which the railway authorities in fixing rates on a railway, have taken into consideration the amount of stock or bonds that had been issued. I am speaking in the presence of the late hon. Minister of Railways (Hon. Mr. Haggart), and he can correct me if I am wrong. We have nothing to do with railways in the United States, and I am not speaking of street railways ; I am speaking of railways which are under the control of this government. I would refer the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) to the 29th paragraph of this agreement, which says :
The rates and tolls to be levied and taken by the company on any part of the said rail-

way shall be under the control of the Governor in Council or of such authority or tribunal as is designated under any Act of the parliament of Canada for the control of the business of the railway.
Surely, any person who takes any of the bonds or the stock of this railway, takes it with a full knowledge that the government, or the tribunal that is constituted by this parliament for that purpose, has the absolute control over fixing rates. Does he mean to tell me that the government or the tribunal which is constituted are foolish enough to have their decision warped in the slightest degree by the amount of stock or bonds put on the market ?
Most decidedly.

Then I must say that he has small confidence in the government, at which I am not surprised, and small confidence in the i tribunal that will be organized; but surely the hon. gentleman who sits beside him will not agree with him in that assumption. The hon. gentleman knows that if the company place the stock at anything less than par, under the law, the holders of the stock will be liable to pay the balance in case it shall be necessary. In this case, in order that the government or the tribunal may not be deceived, the 19th section of the agreement gives the government the most absolute power to investigate in any way they see fit, by the employment of engineers, accountants and inspectors, to ascertain just how much money has been put into the construction of the road. In addition, they have a director sitting at the board of the company, and having access to all its books. If $25,000,000 of this stock were allotted to the Grand Trunk Railway Company on payment of 10 per cent, they would be liable, in case of necessity, to pay the other 90 per cent, and there can be no injury to anyone.

Let me point out an instance which will meet the hon. gentleman's argument. If the government undertook to regulate the rates of this road, it would be in the way of the company being cited to show cause why the rates should not be reduced. The company would say, ' we have issued $45,000,000 of stock.' This may have been purchased by investors for little or nothing ; but in the meantime it may have changed hands, and the old argument of the widow and the orphan would come up again. The Toronto Street Railway pays dividends on $6,000,000 of watered stock, and that fact is the great stumbling block in the way of a reduction of fares. We have asked what consideration the Grand Trunk Railway Company are to pay for this stock. If it is the intention that they shall pay cash for it, and that the money shall go into the treasury of this company, it will go a long way towards building the road. If the money goes in,
value will come from it; but if it is to be watered stock on which dividends are expected to be paid, there will be very little hope of a reduction of rates subsequently.

My hon. friend from Annapolis (Mr. Wade) has apparently examined the proceedings before the Railway Commission of the United States, or he would not have made such a sweeping statement as he has made.

On the contrary, 1 said I was not referring to any proceedings in the United States, but I was confining myself to the proceedings in Canada. I am not familiar with the laws or practice in the United States.
Mr. BORDEN (Halifax.) While the hon. gentleman asserts that it would be childish to take that argument into consideration, American publications say that it is an argument that has been made there again and again before tribunals having power to fix rates, and an argument to which effect has been given. Therefore, when he makes the broad assertion that no one but a child would rely on that argument, he is casting an imputation on gentlemen who have as much familiarity with railways and as much capacity to make an argument as any hon. gentleinan in this House.

If a man gets any of this stock for nothing, he has notice that there will be control over the rates, and the fact that lie holds a par value of $100 for which he gave nothing cannot be given as a reason for keeping up the rates.
I should not think the question of notice would arise in such a case at all. Every one holds stock subject to the general law of the land.
And surely subject to a specific contract under which the stock was purchased.

I cannot grasp my hon. friend's point. All I am suggesting is that when this matter comes before the tribunal having power to deal with rates, this argument, which has been made over and over again in the past, will be repeated, namely, that the company whose rates are sought to be controlled is capitalized at such an amount, and that it is fairly entitled to have its rates fixed, so that it can pay a legitimate profit to the persons who hold the stock. That is an argument which is not affected by any question of notice, so far as I understand it. With regard to the other point, that the Grand Trunk Railway Company are bound to pay $25,000,000 in cash in any possible event, I do not see how that can be made good, in view of the fact that section 11 provides exactly the contrary-that there may be some cases in which stock can be given for considerations which are not cash.

There is no statute requiring the rates to lie fixed according to the amount of the capital stock. Therefore, the only reason why the tribunal would take the amount of the capital stock into account would be that the tolls or rates should be put at such a level as to enable the capital put into the undertaking to be remunerative. If that be the reason, is it not open to the tribunal, which we appoint to fix the rates, to ascertain the true amount of capital and not take the nominal value, especially when those who take the stock take It knowing that a contract exists between the company and the government, providing that the tolls shall be regulated by the tribunal and that the government shall have power to investigate in order to ascertain what the true amount of the investment is. With respect to the contribution, I do not think it is argued that the contribution should be in cash for the stock. It may be in the equivalent to cash. The company will have to give something equivalent to cash in return for the stock.
What is that ?
Plant, rolling stock, elevators, wharfs, warehouses, vessels or materials of any kind. That is what the statute says. If they do not give an equivalent in cash they would have to pay the cash.

My hon. friend has made it very plain now. The intention is exactly what we suspected all along. They are to give the capital stock in return for rolling stock, vessels and services and so on. due regard being had to the market value of the stock. And if the stock would not have any particular market value they could give $25,000,000 of stock for almost nothing and no one could find any fault. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice has made the matter extremely plain.
If I have satisfied the leader of the opposition, I am quite happy.

I desire to call attention to a provision which was in the General Act respecting railways as first introduced, but which was subsequently struck out by the committee, and which is now in the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Bill with a very significant addition. In the General Railway Act, as originally introduced, there was this clause, which was struck out after discussion in this committee.
59. The directors of the company, elected by the shareholders, may make and issue, as paid up stock, shares in the company, whether subscribed for or not, and may allot and hand over such stock in payment for right of way, plant, rolling stock or materials of any kind, and also for the services of contractors and engineers ; and such issue and allotment of stock shall be binding on the company, and such stock shall not be assessable for calls.

After discussion, that clause was struck out. But now we find in this special charter that same clause, which was considered improper to be inserted in the General Railway Act, and in addition certain very significant words :
11. The directors of the company, elected by the shareholders, may make and issue as paid up stock, shares in the company, whether subscribed for or not, and may allot and hand over such stock in payment for plant rolling stock, docks, elevators, wharfs, warehouses, vessels or materials of any kind-
Now comes a very important addition :
. Or as consideration for rights, powers and privileges acquired and also for bona fide claims, &e.
I need not go on with the clause, but here are the significant words : As consideration for rights, powers and privileges acquired. Why, Sir, does this House overlook the fact that the board of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway and the board of the Grand Trunk Railway are one; that when the president of the Grand Trunk Railway sits in his office and shakes hands with the president of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, he shakes his own hand ; that when these two companies sit down together, under another clause of the General Railway Act, and make arrangements for the interchange of traffic and all those other things so common among railway companies, the one company can give to the other rights, powers and privileges, the value of which no one can estimate or weigh ; that if they agree that these rights and privileges are worth $25.000,000 or $25 no man could say it was right or wrong, and that the Grand Trunk Railway may stipulate, in any traffic arrangements which it shall make with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, that $25,000,000 of common stock of the latter road shall be transferred as a consideration for entering into the agreement. How is any railway commission to say that such a bargain is fraudulent or that they paid more or less than the value of the bargain ; and yet, under this clause, with these words in it. which was rejected from the General Railway Act, these two companies may agree that $25.000,000 of common stock shall be considered the equivalent of the contract entered into between them and be considered paid up stock not assessable for calls.
My hon. friend has discovered a mare's nest. He knows that this same clause was standing in the old Railway Act.
No.

Yes. The ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Haggart) stood up in his place, when this clause in the General Railway Bill was objected to. and said that it was similar to the one in the Railway Act.
You have added words which make it entirely different.
The words I have quoted are not in the old Railway Act, namely, ' in consideration for rights, powers and privileges acquired.' These have been inserted for the purposes of this Bill.

My friend knows that when this clause was before the committee, the point now taken by him was not urged. The clause was in the General Railway Bill and also in this Bill, so that the point sought to be made by the hon. member for Hamilton that it was specially introduced in this Bill to make up for something that has been struck out of the General Railway Bill is incorrect. Although there have been some words added, they are simply words which require to be added because this company, as the hon. member for Jacques Cartier has pointed out, is going to erect docks, warehouses and vessels. Therefore the clause is not a departure from the law as it has been since 1888, in section 39 of the Railway Act, which was passed in that year. This company is to provide terminal facilities both upon the Atlantic and upon the Pacific. Therefore, the bonding privilege and the stock they ask to be allowed to issue is not exosbitant. But the hon. gentleman (Mr. Barker) seeks to draw a red herring across the scent by speaking of the president of one company making a bargain with the other company simply by shaking hands with himself. Why, what has been the clamour in the country up to the present time until this contract was announced to the public? It has been that irresponsible people wiere behind this scheme. We had it day after day in the press that the Grand Trunk Railway Com-papny of Canada was not prepared to back this scheme financially. And now this is answered conclusively when it is shown beyond the shadow of a doubt that the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada is behind this scheme financially and every other way. Why, then, should we have the hon. gentleman saying that a bargain between these two companies will be made by the simple process of the chairman of both shaking hands with himself ? This is entirely opposed to the criticism to which the Bill was subjected in the committee. And it is unfair criticism. The desire of the whole country was that the Grand Trunk Railway Company of Canada should take part in this scheme and give it stability. What we have before us is not section 11 or section 13 ; the question is whether $45,000,000 capitalization-having regard to the general legislation which has passed this parliament-is fair or unfair in the casie of a company such as this. And hon. gentlemen are discussing extraneous matters in trying to lead us to the consideration of other sections of the Bill,
which have already been discussed and passed.

I thought I was discussing the question of the capital stock of the company, and I am very much mistaken if I have said a word outside of that subject. The hon. gentleman (Mr. McCarthy) says correctly that in the General Railway Act, as introduced, there was the clause that I more than once called attention to in this House as a very objectionable one, as enabling a company to issue capital stock without getting any money for it. After lengthy discussion the Minister of Railways voluntarily withdrew that clause as one that he did not think it proper to allow to remain in the General Railway Act. But the hon. member for North Sim-coe (Mr. McCarthy) rather gets outside the line of the argument. He says that that clause was in the General Railway Act during the discussion of the clause in this Bill in the Railway Committee, and therefore there was nothing extraordinary in that clause. But the bon. gentleman has overlooked that I pointed out to him that there were very important words incorporated in this clause in this special Bill that was never in the General Railway Act at all ; and it happens that the ' very words that are introduced into this Bill that are peculiarly fitted as between two railway companies allied as these two are, to enable one to issue a large amount of capital stock to the other without getting a dollar out for it. The particular words I referred to were not in the General Railway Act at all ; they are ' or as consideration for rights, powers and privileges acquired.' That is, one railway company may issue stock as fully paid up when it acquires from the other powers and privileges. Why, that is the very point we are raising, that the Grand Trunk Pacific, by entering into an arrangement with the Grand Trunk may acquire privileges of unknown value, and as consideration for them may hand over its common stock. You cannot measure in dollars, or in any way, the value of privileges accorded by one great company to another for the interchange of traffic, the use of terminals and all the other things that a company fifty years of age can offer to a youngster just coming into existence. And, I ask, when these hon. gentlemen were drawing a clause in the terms of the General Railway Act and for this very purpose, why did they not adopt the clause in the General Railway Act as it stood at the time. They inserted all the provisions there, and they added these particular words that never appeared in the General Railway Act. If they have any object at all, it is to enable the Grand Trunk Pacific to give this enormous amount of common stock as compensation for the privileges they propose to gain from the Grand Trunk. Now, I would like the hon. gentleman (Mr. McCarthy), as

he is so ready to answer me and so ready to charge me with using unfair arguments, to explain how these words came to be inserted and who inserted them. Was it the hon. gentleman himself ? He introduced the Bill and has been in charge of it; perhaps he will tell us with what motive these particular words were inserted. Surely the clause that had been in the General Railway Act since 1888 was sufficient for all purposes. Why did they want to insert these words in this particular Act except for the purpose that I have suggested ? And if they wanted the power to deal with the rights and powers and privileges that one company can accord to the other, I think it is a reasonable argument for hon. gentlemen on this side of the House-particularly when you take this provision in connection with the fact that $25,000,000 of common stock is to be acquired from one company to the other company- that this stock is to be given, and, on the other hand, this clause 11 provides for the consideration.

I desire to say just a few words in reply to the hon. gentleman for Annapolis (Mr. Wade). I am glad to see that that hon. gentleman has arrived at the same conclusion that I have often expressed in this House, that the Railway Commission which we are creating will be empowered to inquire into the actual cash expenditure on the road, and fix the charges on that basis. But the hon. member differs entirely in his conclusion from the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) and the Postmaster General (Sir "William Mulock). How often, before the Railway Committee have these hon. gentlemen urged the reduction of the powers to issue stock and the bonding powers of the several railroads under consideration on the very principle that my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) has urged-that the amount of capitalization, including bonds, would be a consideration with the commission in fixing {be rates of the road. I have again and again contended for what the hon. member for Annapolis now says, that the issue of bonds and the issue of stock is an internal affair that concerns the company itself and is independent of any legislation that we may enact in reference to fixing of rates ; that the true criterion is the amount of cash expended on the road, and that on the basis of this cjtsh expenditure the commission should fix the rates. I do not say that the capitalization of this road is too large when we consider that all the rolling stock of the road is to be arranged on the western section, and that the powers of bonding are confined to that section. They have to build the section of the road from Winnipeg to Lake Superior, they have to build the connection between the main line and North Bay, and-whether they ever intend to build it or not-to make the connection
with a railway that centres in Montreal. If they intend to do all these things the capitalization is not too large. But, unfortunately for the consideration of this subject, the hon. member who lias charge of the Bill did not explain that feature of it. He confined his explanations to the government section of the road, and the road which the company intend to build from Winnipeg to the ocean. He did not seem to know that capital was required for the purpose of building these sections of the road. I am not opposed to the Bill at all. Give the Grand Trunk Railway Company the fullest power to enable them to fulfil the bargain they have entered into with the government. When you give them that power, then we will discuss the bargain they have made with the government. But, we cannot shut our eyes to the statement of my hon. friend from Hamilton (Mr. Barker), where he draws attention to the extraordinary powers given in section 11. I have stated before that it empowered the Grand Trunk Railway Company to make an arrangement with this new corporation which enabled them, in exchange for the guarantees which they give for the rolling stock that is put upon the road-or, as my hon. friend says, in pursuance of any other family or private arrangement made between the two companies-to give this stock over to the Grand Trunk Railway Company. Now, the question must occur, how is the Grand Trunk Railway Company to raise the $25,000,000 ?
