The hon. gentleman is entirely wrong.

The Postmaster General takes a map and lie draws a line on it, and looks at the scale and figures up the distance. He has never traversed that country up north. We have heard the statement made by the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Talbot) who, though speaking in favour of another road, said it was impossible to cross the line of country south of the height of land on account of the mountains, that it was impossible to get a line to run east and west, and that the only possible route from Quebec to the great west was away north of the height of land, 100 miles north of the line drawn by my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk). The Postmaster General, I suppose, takes a line from the end of this Montreal and Western Railway to the point drawn on the map by the member for Jacques Cartier, which is 75 miles by the scale, and you can easily add 20 per cent to that for the devious windings of the hills. There is another point. Why should the government employ a roving commission to build a line from Gravenhurst to some imaginary point on the Grand Trunk Railway through a country over which they already have a road to North Bay, a country in which construction is now going on in connection with the James Bay Railway, and in which the Canadian Pacific Railway is at present, it may be. preparing to construct a railway 1 In other words, they are going to endeavour to cripple both the Canadian Pacific Railway and the James Bay Railway ; and even if this branch from Gravenhurst is never built, it will be held as a whip over the heads of these other two companies in order to depreciate their bonds in the markets of the world. Why should the government insert that word ' Gravenhurst ' in this agreement ?

In looking over this agreement I fail to see any provision made for a connection with the city of St. John, except the connection by way of the Intercolonial by Moncton. I understood, when the matter was discussed before, that there was to be a connection in another way, by Chipman. I would like to ask from the promoter of the Bill what is the intention, why that was left out, or whether it was an oversight.
I have no information.

It seems to me that is rather an important matter. The city of St. John is one of the most important of our Atlantic seaports, and if this railway is to be any good at all it should give the shortest possible connection with the sea. and that certainly cannot be made by going away round by Moncton. I understood both the member for Annapolis (Mr. Wade) and the Minister of Justice to say that the shortest way to get to St. John frdm Moncton was not by way of the Intercolonial, but by way of Chipman. I would not think so much of that, coming* from the Minister of Justice, because living so far away from Sir WILLIAM MULOCK.
New Brunswick, he would not be well posted in the geography of that province. But the member for Annapolis surely would be expected to know something about it, and according to him it is easier to go to St. John by way of Chipman than by way of Moncton, direct by the Intercolonial.

What I said was that there was a shorter way over this line of railway to St. John than by way of Moncton to St. John. I mean that you go off the main line at a point near Chipman, and go to the nearest point on the Intercolonial on its way to St. John, which is a point about 33 miles to the east of St. John. Norton is the name of the place.
There is no such provision in this agreement.
Is there any provision that it shall go to Halifax ?

I think I was right in understanding that the intention was not to take any shorter course from the main line of this road to St. John than by going to Moncton and from there down by the Intercolonial.
You would save 50 miles.
It is possible to save fifty miles.

Assuming that we have power to build from L6vis to Edmundston, then starting from Edmunds-ton, would it not be almost a direct line to go by Chipman, which would be a common point to Moncton and St. John ?
Mr.. FOWLER. No, you could make it much shorter by not going to Chipman at all.
If the committee would allow me, I would add a clause to build from a point on the government line so as to approach Chipman. or if necessarv, go to St. John.

Why not provide to go to St. John by the shortest possible route from Edmundston, if you want to strike St. John by the shortest line ? Why not cut across, because it would be much shorter than to go around the triangle ? If you take your route from Edmundston and' go down the St. John valley you will get a much shorter line.
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) The hon. member for Lanark (Hon. Mr. Haggart) and the hon. member for King's, N.B. (Mr. Fowler) have stated emphatically that the Intercolonial Railway from Moncton to Halifax is the shortest possible route. There are eminent engineers whose names I might mention who would state emphatically that the road could be shortened at least fifty miles. The road was run up to the Spring-hill Mines, where it hugs the side of the mountain for the purpose of being near the

mines. Theii, it went down to suit the interests of Peter Mitchell to Chatham and Newcastle.
Mr. IxAULBACH. The Grecian Bend.
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) Yes, the Grecian Bend. If you follow that route on the Grecian Bend you can stand on the platform of one of the front cars, and you will see the cars behind, because the road is so crooked; whereas, if the line had followed the valley below, it would have found a natural level country to traverse. I know something about the history of that road. If Sir Leonard Tilley had had his own way the road would not have been built by that route, and it would have been shortened considerably, but Peter Mitchell was one of those Scotchmen who was bound to have his own way, he bad a following from northern New Brunswick, and the road was diverted away from the proper route. Those who will assert that the road from Moncton to Halifax is the shortest possible route are speaking of something they know nothing at all about.

The Mitchell influence which the hon. member for Victoria (Hon. Mr. Ross) refers to certainly would not affect the route from Moncton to Halifax. That influence would only secure the adoption of the route along the north shore instead of down the valley of St. John, where Sir Leonard Tilley wished it to go. But, as far as the route from Moncton to Halifax is concerned, if you take the map and draw the straightest line that you can from Moncton to Halifax, you cannot affect a saving of fifty miles or anything like that, and of course, there are engineering difficulties which would prevent you from making a straight line if you wanted to.
On the contrary, you will escape the engineering difficulties.

Not at all. It is about 180 miles, or under 200 miles, from Moncton to Halifax, and you cannot affect a saving of anything like fifty miles even by following a straight line. As far as the southern district is concerned, if the promoter of the Bill wishes to add an amendment, the only amendment that would be practicable would be one providing for a route starting from Edmundston and going in the most direct course to the city of St. John.
Hon. Mr. ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) I have the authority of the most eminent engineers for what I have said.
Do I understand from the promoter that the contract entered into between the company and the government does not compel the building of a branch line to the head of Lake Superior?
I do not think the contract refers to it at all. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Roche) has the contract before him.

If the contract does not provide for connection with Lake Superior as far as this road is concerned, it will not fill the bill as affecting the movement of wheat from the west, because an all-rail route cannot hope to compete with a rail and water route, and there will be mighty little grain to come down over this all-rail route to an Atlantic seaport. Unless there is a connection with Lake Superior, it will not afford the relief to the western people that it is supposed that this road will afford. Even with connection with Lake Superior, it will be at a disadvantage, because the route as mapped out north of Lake Nepigon is 100 miles or 150 miles north of Lake Superior. If there is not going to be compulsory connection with Lake Superior, in so far as the commercial aspect of the line is concerned this route will not relieve the congestion of the grain traffic that we have been feeling for the last two years in the west, and the people of the west will not approve of this large expenditure of money when it will not afford them the relief which they so much desire.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Roche, Marquette) seems to be labouring under a misapprehension. There is no doubt that it is the intention to build to Lake Superior. That was provided for in the original clause, but since the main line is to be built by the government it is necessary to amend it so as to give this company power to build a branch line to reach Lake Superior. It is clearly the intention of the company to build a branch line to Lake Superior.
Do I understand the promoter floes not propose to make this amendment in respect to St. John? The hon. gentleman has changed his mind.

I did not say that I could ask for any amendment other than I have asked for now unless it was prepared by the solicitor for the company, who knows what the railway company wants and the amendment which the company wants is the amendment which is now before the committee.

But the amendment which is before the committee does not speak of St. John at all.
Mr. McCarthy. No.

What amendment did you propose to offer ? You say that I am asking too much because I want you to go by way of the shortest line. Do you propose to amend the section by making the route shorter, but not the shortest ? I cannot understand the position which the hon. gentleman takes. Have I wounded his feelings in any way by standing up

for the best interests of the province which I represent, or does he refuse to grant that measure of relief to the people of St. John which a moment ago he himself admitted that they deserved? Surely my hon. friend does not consider the matter in any personal way. I was trying to promote the interests of a portion of the people of the province of New Brunswick and of St. John, and it does seem to me that the hon. gentleman, who was going to grant this measure of relief, should not withdraw it simply because I asked more than he is willing to grant.

The hon. gentleman overpowers me with the greatness that he seeks to thrust upon me. I am only in charge of this Bill in the House. The amendment* which the company thought would afford them the relief they desired is before the House. I have nothing to do with it. All I have are the instructions which I have received as to this. Personally I would he glad to grant relief to the whole Dominion, and particularly to the part which the hon. gentleman represents, but I have nothing to do with it. The amendments are making necessary corrections in the original line which was approved by the committee, of the Grand Trunk Pacific, but by reason of the government undertaking the building of the road from Winnipeg to Moncton, I have to get this proviso inserted allowing branch lines to be built. That is all that is asked for by the company.

I was not thrusting any greatness upon the hon. gentleman. There are said to be three classes, some who are born great, others who achieve greatness and others who have greatness thrust upon them, but the hon. gentleman belongs to a fourth class. He assumes greatness. The hon. gentleman said that he would amend his amendment by providing that there should be a branch line from some point on the main line leading from Moncton to St. John. But, now he goes back upon that, and the reason he gives for going back upon it is because I suggested to him that instead of branching off at Chipman, he should branch off at the main line before he came to Chipman, because in so doing he would get a shorter route to the city of St. John. The hon. gentleman has given a puerile reason for now refusing to grant the small measure of relief which he was willing to give some time ago. It seems to me that the hon. gentleman may have been inspired by an authority higher than himself to change his mind. I hope it is not because of a whisper from the Minister of Justice nor the Minister of Finance or the Minister of Labour by whom he is surrounded.

We must start with the idea that it cannot be left to my hon. friend (Mr. McCarthy) or to any Mr. FOWLER.
other member to determine what we shall have or what we shall not have in the Bill ; the committee must take upon itself to decide that. The situation is this : It is the intention of the government to construct the line from Winnipeg-to Moncton and in connection with that line it was thought desirable to give to the company the right to construct branch lines for the purpose of reaching commercial centres. The first of these centres after leaving Winnipeg, is Fort William, then Port Arthur and North Bay, and finally Montreal. When we leave Quebec after crossing the river, the line goes to Edmunds-ton and from Edmundston to Moncton, and between these two points there will be a branch to the city of St. John just as there is a branch to other cities on the western end of this section. I understand that has been in the mind of the Minister of Finance for some time. It has been considered and discussed, and I cannot see any reason why, if the committee wishes it, we should not authorize that company to build that line to St. John.
I am very glad to have the support of the Minister of Justice for my contention.

This is a very serious proposition. The government proposes to build the line from Winnipeg to Monpton, but the Bill now before this committee is not the scheme that we considered in the Railway Committee. To-night we have before us a railway to be constructed by the government and to be owned by the government from Winnipeg to Moncton, but the scheme before the Railway Committee was a proposition of the Grand Trunk Railway Company to build a national transcontinental railway. It is now proposed that we should give our sanction to the building of a number of branches, and that is altogether outside of the line of the project which was reported to this House by the Railway Committee and which I submit is the only subject which this House has now a right to consider. We are not in a position to-night, and we will not be in a position to decide on any such scheme as is now proposed until this Bill goes back to the Railway Committee and is there considered in its new aspect. The branches were not included in the Bill which we considered in the Railway Committee and their consideration is not properly before this House to-night. All that is left of what went before the Railway Committee is the building of the line by the Lrand Trunk Pacific Railway from Winnipeg west to the Pacific ocean. Ill-defined as the whole scheme is, more ill-defined still is that scheme to build branch lines, and yet we are asked to sanction this indefinite scheme although it never came before the Railway Committee of this House. I do not want to throw any barriers in the way, but I want to have the question treated in a logical sense and in the light of the responsibility which we owe to the people. If

the government is going to build the line from Winnipeg to Moncton why on earth can not they build the branches as well ? It was said the other day that we had a hybrid scheme before us, but what kind of a scheme is this which comes up for consideration to-night ? We have the trunk line from Winnipeg to Moncton built by the government; we have the western end built by the Grand Trunk Railway, and we have proposed to-night a lot of little feeders to be built by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway to the national line constructed by the government. I venture to say that the feeders in the end will be the people of Canada and not the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. Therefore, I protest with all the force I can against this uncertain and indeterminate kind of partnership and mixup which is proposed between the government and the Grand Trunk Railway Company.

I desire to ask that the word ' Gravenhurst ' be dropped out of the proposed amendment, inasmuch as there is one line of the Grand Trunk Railway already constructed to North Bay, and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company are about to complete their own line from Toronto to connect with their main line at or near Sudbury. Then, there is still another road under construction, the James Bay Railway, from Toronto to Parry Sound, and connecting with the Northern road a little west of Wahnapitae. The insertion of this word ' Gravenhurst,' giving this company a roving commission to construct a line from that point to some point on their main line, will materially affect these other companies when they go to the markets of the world to raise money. I presume that the hon. member in charge of the Bill has no objection to drop the word ' Gravenhurst.'

I cannot consent to the hon. gentleman's suggestion, in view of the suggestion of the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) that this road is not the shortest route from the west to Toronto, and for other reasons.

The cut-off from North Bay to this Arctic road would answer as well as a cut-off from Gravenhurst. I am satisfied that if this Bill went before the Railway Committee, that committee, with the non-partisan spirit it has always displayed, would not allow-it to parallel all these other roads ; and if the hon. member in charge of the Bill will not consent to withdraw the word * Gravenhurst,' I will ask the sense of the committee upon the question, and will move that this Bill be referred back to the Railway Committee, which I am satisfied would not tolerate any such iniquity.
Mr. McCarthy. Looking at the map, 1 cannot see that the proposed road will parallel either the Canadian Pacific Railway or what the hon. gentleman calls the James Bay Railway, which I presume is a part of tlie Mackenzie & Mann proposed transcontinental line, which I understand is neither under construction or located to Winnipeg. It will not parallel these lines, but will cut across them.

The hon. gentleman, I suppose never took a prize in geography. Certainly the knowledge he has displayed in geography would not entitle him to rank as first-class.
Mr. McCarthy. Not if you were the examiner.

I have myself seen the survey parties of the Canadian Pacific Railway within the past six weeks, and I learned from them that their work of locating their line was nearly completed. I dare say that the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, with a little more foresight than this government, make surveys before they undertake to construct a line. The hon. gentleman speaks of the James Bay Railway as not being surveyed. It is surveyed to upwards of a hundred miles north of Wahnapitae. I move that the word 'Gravenhurst' be omitted.

What the hon. member who has just sat down has said has emphasized the necessity of pressing on the committee the point I take. I understood that the proposal to charter the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway from Moncton to Winnipeg was struck out of the Bill. I am told by a member of the committee who has followed the discussion this afternoon, that this is not the case, and that it is proposed to charter this company to run a line from Moncton to Winnipeg. I ask the promoter of the Bill if that is correct ?
I presume the hon. gentleman has read the amendment ?

I understand, then, that that is not the case. But It does not alter the position I took. Hon. members of the committee should keep this fact clearly in mind, that what was first proposed to the House and discussed in the Railway Committee was not the construction of feeders or branches, but of a national highway from ocean to ocean. If there had been a question, in the Railway Committee, of constructing these feeders, we would then have considered the question of paralleling or interfering with existing charters. We would have considered the whole question on a broader basis than was necessary under the Bill as presented to the Railway Committee. The committee have referred to this House the Bill to build a trunk line from ocean to ocean, and we have not now the right to initiate what is. to all intents and purposes, a new Bill, but must confine ourselves to the proposition' debated

in the Railway Committee. All that we have the right to deal with is that portion of the road which the government have not decided to build, namely, from Winnipeg to Port Simpson. These branch lines are, therefore, out of the question. The government does not propose to build from Winnipeg to the Pacific, so that that portion of the charter is properly before this committee. This is the crucial point, namely, that the question of building these branches was never brought before the Railway Committee and never considered by them.
Look at the main clause.

If it was considered by the committee, why bring in an amendment now ? If it was considered by the committee and rejected-
Mr. McCarthy. Never.
Then there is no ground for bringing it in.

If the hon. gentleman will look at the main part of section 12 he will find that the idea was that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway should construct from Winnipeg to Moncton and build branches. But now that the government are going to construct from Winnipeg to Moncton, it is deemed necessary to provide that these branch lines should be built.

I cannot see it in that light, because if it were considered by the Railway Committee and not rejected by that committee, it would be in the Bill as reported by that committee to the House, and there would be no necessity for that amendment. But what the promoter of the Bill is proposing is some scheme that was never considered by the Railway Committee, I therefore must protest against any such attempt in the strongest possible manner.

A suggestion has been made to the effect that a line should be provided from Edmundston to St. John. That, in my judgment, would be very impracticable, and would not serve the interest of the city of St. John as they would be served by the amendment I am about to propose. Chipman is a common point, and from that point it would be in the interests of the country to reach St. John by the nearest possible route. From Chipman there is today a line connecting at Norton on the Intercolonial Railway with the city of St. John. I would move that these words be added to the section :
Also build a branch line from the main line at a point at or near Chipman to St. John, or to acquire any existing branch lines which may serve the -same purpose.
That amendment would be in the interests of the whole Dominion as it would give the shortest possible route to an Atlantic port.

I must take exception to the remarks of the hon. member for Westmoreland. His amendment would be most unfair to the province of Nova Scotia inasmuch as Chipman is very far south of a direct line drawn from Edmundston to Moncton, and that point (Moncton) could be reached very much more conveniently by a shorter line which would cost the government less than the route which the hon. member proposes.
This is the company, not the government.

The government have to pay for it all the same. I know very little of New Brunswick as respects the route which the proposed company intend to take, but I gather my knowledge from a geographical sketch taken from the map of Nejv Brunswick and Quebec. There are very many engineering difficulties almost insurmountable on the route between Quebec and Moncton. First of all, I would say, I am utterly opposed to the Intercolonial Railway being paralleled. Again I am opposed to that proposed line of road between Quebec and Moncton running to Edmundston, because it brings us too close to the American border. I object to it for the same reason that I object to the Canadian Northern going through the state of Minnesota to the city of Winnipeg. But, if the proposed road is to be taken from Quebec to Edmundston. I do not see why the Intercolonial should not be utilized as far as River Du Loup, and then take the Temiseouata road to Edmundston and in a straight line from Edmundston to Newcastle and then utilize the straight line from Newcastle to Moncton. If you look at the map, you will see that this is almost a straight line. But if you take the road to Chipman, you make an angle, and a divergence which would be saved in taking the line from Edmundston to Moncton via Newcastle. Going from Edmundston you will reach Newcastle almost as quickly as you reach Chipman, and the distance from Newcastle to Moncton, I think, is no more than 70 miles.
Order.
If I am not keeping within tbe rules, Mr. Chairman, I am wiling to take my seat, but I think I am not digressing more than some hon. gentlemen who. have preceded me.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I did not call the hon. member (Mr. Kaulbach) to order.

I thought the voice was yours, sir. I think that my hon. friend from Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) is quite wrong when be asks that the road should go to Chipman, because it would make the road from Chipman to Moncton considerably longer than if it ran direct

from Edmundston to Newcastle and thence by the Intercolonial to Moncton.

I do not understand why the hon. gentleman (Mr. Emmerson), if he is sincere, if his solicitude for the best interest of the city of St. John is as great as it appears, should object to this branch road going from Edmundston to St. John. Take your main line from Moncton by the most direct route, but let the branch line from Edmundston go down the valley of St. John along the old line of the Intercolonial, the line approved by Sir Leonard Tilley, but in which he was overruled by Mr. Mitchell, according to traditions of those days. Let your branch line run from there, and you need not deflect your main line from Chipman at all, but go by more direct route, as the hon. member from Lunenburg (Mr. Kaulbach) has pointed out, than if you deflected your main line in order to strike Chipman. That would serve the interest of St. John better, and that large and important section of the province which has now no railway, the valley of St. John, it would serve efficiently, and would be found perfectly practicable and would give a shorter route to St. John than if you go across the province to Chipman and thence to St. John. You have to go by Norton and down to St. John by way of the Intercolonial, which is a long way, making two sides of a triangle, whereas if you go direct from Moncton you make only one side of the triangle.

I took the trouble, on a former occasion, to demonstrate to the committee discussing this matter that if you were to attempt to go to St. John by way of Chipman, you would have to travel only 37 miles more than you would if you were to follow the valley of St. John and go into St. John, landing on the west side of the harbour along the line of the Canadian Pacific Railway. I also endeavoured to show that when you reach the western side of the harbour you are in a place where the harbour rights and terminal facilities are almost exclusively held by the Canadian Pacific Railway, and that for such a road as this it is absolutely necessary to get access to the harbour of St. John op the east side, in what is known as St. John East. . In order to get harbour facilities and terminal facilities in St. John, it would be necessary to utilize the property on the east side of the harbour. Hon. members know that there is a bridge company which controls the bridge over the falls. That has been a great barrier to the traffic of the city of St. John. The tolls have been very large, as they have a monopoly, and have a branch line running from their bridge into St. John. This has been considered a very serious obstacle to the trade between St. John and the western section of the country. To go by way of Chipman would be only 37 miles farther, and it would bring you into St.' John on
the east side of the harbour, where there is every opportunity for terminal and harbour facilities. I would say to my hon. friend from King's (Mr. Fowler) that it was only within a very few years that a survey was made by, I think, the Ternis-couata Railway, and under the direction of or in connection with the Grand Trunk, as I understand. That survey, the latest made of that country, shows the selected route from Edmundston down to a point at or near Chipman and running across from Chipman to the Intercolonial somewhere between Moncton and Salisbury. That route is considered the shortest, though it is not the best route that is to be found. My hon. friend from Lunenburg speaks of going down to Newcastle. But he must realize that the topographical conditions would make that utterly impracticable. He would find obstacles like the Nipisiquit lakes, and the Bald mountains, and others between the waters of Tobique and the Nipisiquit rivers. If you could go as the crow flies, it would be all right. But you must recognize the topographical conditions in the way and, recognizing these conditions, I think that all hon. members of the commit-eet will realize that the only route possible would be from Edmundston down more through the centre of the province. You could not deviate to the north to any great extent. My hon. friend from King's knows that, and he knows also that any line down through the centre of the province would bring him near Chipman-

No.
Air. EMA1ERSON. It might be a few miles away. But when they were seeking the shortest line they located it a few miles back of Chipman.

A long way.
Air. EA1A1ERSON. I have seen the survey, and I have discussed the matter with the gentlemen on the survey, so that my information is direct. So it would be at a point at or near Chipman. There is a wilderness between Chipman and the head of the waters known as the Salmon river, on the main highway between Chipman and Har-eourt, on the road leading to Richibucto in the county of Kent. I have travelled over that line and am familiar with the topography of the country ; I know the conditions which would make it necessary to pass in the vicinity of Chipman. Now after reaching Chipman, it would be in the interest of the company operating that line to take a cut of 70 miles to the city of St. John rather than go a like distance to Aloncton and then travel back oyer their tracks SO miles to St. John. If you went from Chipman to Aloncton and turned back to St. John you would go a distance of 150' miles. By means of this branch which the company is seeking power to build, or acquire, they can go into St. John from Chip-man, a distance of about 70 miles, saving 90

miles in reaching St. John. To go by the line indicated by the hon. member from King's (Mr. Fowler), you would travel down the valley of St. John to Fredericton, then there would be two ways open for you if you wished to keep on the western bank of the river St. John. You might follow down the western bank by Gagetown as far as Hampstead, and there you would meet barriers all the way which would lengthen your route. It is an impracticable route, as my hon. friends know ; there are hills and mountains to overcome, and there are low lands submerged a month or more every spring, and even during the autumn freshets. Then there is another route by following the Canadian Pacific Railway from Fredericton down to St. John. There again you are met with another difficulty at St. John. You do not shorten your distance, and you are met with the bridge barrier at the harbour ; you are met with a condition of things which make it impossible for this company to secure terminal facilities. The Canadian Pacific Railway have control of what is known as the Carleton branch, they have control of the terminals there, and you would have to go away out into the open, down towards Duck Cove, if you wanted to get larger facilities on that side of the harbour. Now, by this proposed route, if you were to go to Chipman and go down by way of this branch to St. John, you would bring St. John 204 miles nearer to the bridge at Quebec than it is to-day by means of the Intercolonial Railway. You annihilate a distance of 204 miles, and you bring St. John and Quebec that much closer together.
The hon. gentleman is altogether astray in his mileage.

I can prove my figures to a mathematical demonstration, because I know whereof I am speaking. I am calculating from Chaudiere, from a point where the bridge will cross the river at Quebec, and I am showing that from that point to Moncton is 498 miles. From Moncton-and my hon. friend can add the figures together -to St. John is 89 miles. The sum total of that exceeds the distance from ChaudiSre-
What is the entire distance to Chipman ?
To St. John 383 miles by way of Chipman ?
The hon. gentleman cannot make it within 425 miles by way of Chipman.

The distance, by way of the Intercolonial Railway from the point where this bridge crosses the river at Quebec, to St. John, is 587 miles. The distance by the surveys which have been made from that point down to Chipman, and from Chipman down to St. John, is 383 miles. The difference between 383 and 587 is 204 ; that is the saving in distance between those Mr. EMMERSON.
two points. This only goes to show, however, that even if there were a variation of a few miles, there is an annihilation of 200 miles as between these two cities, by the proposed route by way of Chipman, and then down to Norton, thence down to St. John. This amendment proposed by me makes it possible for the company to secure these rights, it makes it possible for St. John to have the advantage of being that much nearer the trunk line, and it makes it not only possible for her to be that much nearer, but it ensures to that city a large proportion of the freight traffic that would come down over that route. Certainly the interests of St. John would be in that direction, the interests of no other section would be injured, and the interests of the company itself and the interest of the transportation facilities of this Dominion are best served by the operation of this branch line.

I wish to point out to the hon. gentleman that from Edmundston it is necessary to parallel the Canadian Pacific Railway all the way down to Grand Falls. You have got to go to Grand Falls before you can get away from the Canadian Pacific Railway.
The topography of the country between Edmundston and Grand Falls is such that it would not permit the construction of a line northward or eastward.

Exactly. I quite understand the reason why. Topographically the country is such that you could not get away from it and you must parallel the Canadian Pacific Railway down almost to Grand Falls. You would need to parallel the Canadian Pacific Railway, also for a short distance going down the western side of the river. As far as terminal facilities are concerned what my hon. friend says respecting the Canadian Pacific Railway having absolute control of the terminal facilities on the western side of the harbour of St. John is scarcely correct, i do not think the Canadian Pacific Railway have any such rights as the hon. gentleman has just stated. The control of the terminal facilities which belong to the city of St. John is in the hands of the city of St. John and these facilities are not under the absolute control of the Canadian Pacific Railway.
The city handed over the Carleton branch irrevocably.

That is very true, but the wharfs and docks which are terminal facilities after all, are still under the control of the city of St. John. There are two elevators belonging to the Canadian Pacific Railway, but there is ample room on the western side of the harbour for facilities for both, and it is only a question of money. As I understand this agreement, the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway are obliged to provide the necessary terminal facilities at all

ports on the Atlantic and Pacific to which their lines run. Therefore, the argument which my hon. friend has made does not affect the case at all and the interest of the port of St. John, which is the commercial centre of a very large portion of the province of New Brunswick, and in the welfare of that city a very large portion of the province is intimately concerned- the interest of the port of St. John will not be served by this road unless it branches off at Edmundston instead of Ohipman, as suggested by my hon. friend. I see the hon. member for the county of St. John (Mr. Tucker), in his seat-unfortunately the hon. member representing the city of St. John is not present, hut X think the hon. member for the county of St. John will bear me out in the statement I have made. I do not think that hon. gentleman will be so recreant to his duty as to agree with the hon. member for Westmoreland that the route which he had proposed by the way of Chipman would be so advantageous to the city of St. John or so advantageous to those represented by himself as the route from Edmundston direct to the city. I quite understand why the hon. member for Westmoreland is so desirous to have this deflection made at Chipman. My hon. friend represented the county of Westmoreland. Moncton is the chief town of that constituency and it is only natural that he should wish that this road should not be lessened in its importance as far as Moncton is concerned by having a shorter route to St. John. By the route which he proposes the line will be ten or fifteen miles nearer to Moncton than to St. John, and that, perhaps, may to some extent account for the desire on the part of the hon. member for Westmoreland to have the branch line start from Chipman rather than from Edmundston. The hon. gentleman must realize himself, if he is honest, that he is influenced by that motive, because such motives do affect us imperceptibly notwithstanding The fact that we may believe we are taking a fair and impartial view of the question. As far as I am concerned, I have no such interest affecting me because my interests would be the other way. If the deflection is made at Chipman a portion of the road would run through my county from Chipman to Norton, and I am looking at what is going to be for the best interests for the country at large, uninfluenced by sectional interests. We want to get the western produce forwarded by the shortest possible route to the Atlantic ocean, and that object can only be achieved by adopting the route which I have suggested, and 1 suggest to the hon. gentleman that he amend his amendment by striking out the word 'Chipman' and inserting 'Edmundston,' and by striking out all after the word ' St. [DOT]John' in his resolution. That will cover the whole case. The Grand Trunk Railway line will go to Moncton in order to
suit hon. members from Nova Scotia, and the hon. member for Westmoreland, but let it branch off at Edmundston and both purposes will be served, besides which the best interests of the province will be served.
It may not be known to the members of this committee that there is already a line from Edmundston to St. John.
There is a line from Quebec to St. John.
There is a line direct down the river St. John from Edmundston to St. John.
Is there not a line from Levis to Edmundston.
There is a line from Rividre du Loup.
There is a line from Levis to Edmundston.

I think there is one thing that the hon. member for King's, New Brunswick (Mr. Fowler) has entirely overlooked and it is a matter which is very material in the discussion of this question. It is of the greatest importance to have a railway that will open up and develop the coal areas in the vicinity of Chip-man and it is of vast importance to the city of St. John that there should be a direct communication such as would be afforded by this line I have suggested in the amendment I have proposed. The hon. member for King's, of course, is very heroic. He does not think of the interest of his constituents. I confess to a desire to contribute in every possible way to the advancement of the section of country from which I come. I do not want it to be done at the sacrifice of any other portion of the Dominion. I want it to be done in the general interest, and the general interest in connection with the transportation facilities of this Dominion demands that there shall be the shortest possible route from Quebec to Moncton affording facilities for the transportation of freight and passenger traffic. The natural outlet for that traffic, or a large portion of it at least, would be by means of a deviation at or near Chipman. Whether it is at Chipman or five miles farther, it makes no difference. The nearest point to the city of St. John is secured by the branch which I have suggested in the amendment now before the committee. It is hardly necessary to take up any more time in the discussion of this matter. The interest of St. John requires it. It would be folly to think of building a line from Edmundston following the route of the present Canadian Pacific Railway. You can go to-day by two different ways to St. John. You can either go down by the Gibson line, on the eastern side of the St. John river, or you can go out from Wood-

stock by way of Me Ada in Junction. These lines connect with Edmundston ; they connect direct with the city of St. John ; and we will simply be building a long line of railway following the tracks of the other line, and we will be affording facilities which are now accorded for transportation between Edmundston and the city of St. John.

It is a strange thing that you should call a railway a transcontinental line which ends at Moncton, which is not a seaport at all. My hon. friend (Mr. Em-merson) has said that you must not build this branch from Edmundston, because there is already a line of railway from Edmundston. Well, there is already a line of railway from Cbipman to the Intercolonial Railway at Norton ; there is a line of railway already projected and chartered this session to connect Chipman with Moncton ; there are lines of railway connecting Quebec with St. John ; there are lines of railway connecting the west with the east ; but is that any argument why there should not be another line of railway ? I am surprised at the very fallacious argument which my hon. friend (Mr. Emmerson) has advanced. He says he is prompted to work on behalf of his constituents. So am I. But when the good of the greater number is concerned, then the good of the smaller number has to give way. It is the duty of a representative of the people in parliament to advocate the best interests of the whole country rather than of any particular section, even though that particular section happens to be the section which he represents, so long as no great injury is done to it.
You would even shut out King's county ?
It is impossible to do that. King's county occupies such a central position in the province of New Brunswick that it has got to be heard from, whether in this House or outside the House.
My hon. friend from Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) is a little astray in his arithmetic with regard to distances.
In his geography, too.
You are a poor schoolmaster.

I confess that I have not that knowledge of the province of New Brunswick that my hon. friend possesses, but at the same time when I look at the map which I have before me, I cannot for the life of me understand how he can say that the shortest line from Quebec to Moncton is via Chipman.

Will my hon. friend pardon me ? The shortest practical route, according to the surveys, is a line through Mr. EMMERSON.
Chipman. As the crow flies possibly you could get shorter, if you built an air line.
What surveys are you referring to ?
I am referring to the last survey made by the Grand Trunk Railway and the Temiscouata road, which I think is the very latest survey, and which was made some eight or ten years ago.

I am safe in saying that if you take the distance from Edmundston down to Chipman and then back to Moncton, that the present Intercolonial Railway is equally as short. I cannot understand why the hon. gentleman would want to go down to Chipman. There is no reason why we should make that diversion and lengthen the distance to Moncton from Edmundston. According to the Intercolonial Railway time-table, the distance saved on the entire proposed new line from Quebec to Moncton is only about 44 miles.
Where did you get that on the Intercolonial Railway time-table ?
By going by way of Riviere du Loup and the Tdmiscouata road, which you would have to take, because you cannot get through the Alleghany range' of mountains
The Alleghanies do not reach there.
There is a line of mountains between the St. Lawrence river and the St. John river of that name.
And these are the Alleghanies.

I am therefore correct. If you want to overcome that range of mountains you must come by Riviere du Loup, take the Temiscouata to Edmundston and straight over as well as you can to Newcastle on the Intercolonial Railway. Then you could utilize the Intercolonial Railway from Newcastle to Moncton. If that course is taken, and I am informed by those who know the country, that it is practicable, it would be the better course to pursue. If my hon. friend will look at the map he will see the distance from Edmundston to Newcastle is shorter than by going to Chipman. The distance from Chipman to Moncton is greater than if you go from Newcastle to Moncton. Under those circumstances, my view is correct as to this route being the shorter of the two.

1 take the liberty of submitting some figures which I have obtained from the most accurate reports available. First I take the figures given by the Prime Minister the other day from Moncton to Edmundston, which he said was on the authority of some survey which I have been unable to find a trace of, but I presume the hon. member for Westmoreland

(Mr. Emmerson) furnished these figures. The Prime Minister stated that the distance from Moncton to Edmundston is 209 miles. The shortest distance to Lfivis is 196 miles, and adding 10 miles to reach the 'bridge that would give you at least 415 miles from Moncton to the Chaudiere bridge. I venture to say that you would have to add at least 10 per cent to that for the 209 miles from Moncton to Edmundston, which would give you 20 miles more, making the total distance 435 miles. Every one who has been in the central part of New Brunswick knows that it is a sea of hills which are worse to get over than mountains.
How do you get your figures from Moncton to Edmundston ?

The Prime Minister stated in his speech that it was 209 miles. It is much more as a matter of fact, but I take his figures. The present Intercolonial Railway is 577 miles from L&vis to St. John. Via Ohipman the route will be 196 miles to Edmundston from Levis, or 206 miles from the Chaudiere bridge to Edmundston and 209 from Edmundston to a junction above Chipman. Then you will find that it is 15 miles farther from Chipman to St. John than it is from Chipman to Moncton. and the road will cross 20 miles north of Chipman. No one pretends that the main line will run into Chipman. Therefore, the saving from Quebec to St. John by the new route compared with the old route will be, at the outside, only 127 miles, and to the city of Moncton a saving of only about 48 or 50 miles.

I wish to move an amendment, that all the words in the amendment of the hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson) after the word ' Chipman ' be struck out, and the word ' Edmundston ' be inserted, and that all the words after the word * St. John ' be struck out.

I think that the hon. member who has charge of the Bill gave notice of his amendment, which is amendment No. 1, and that of the hon. member for Westmoreland is amendment No. 2. My hon. friend puts in a third. I think we shall have to get rid of one of these amendments before we can take up another. I do not wish to press the point, but I think that is the rule.
If the Chair is to stand to the strict rules of order, I think the hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson), did not give notice of his amendment, and therefore it is as much out of order as mine.
My interpretation of the rule is that notice has to be given of an amendment, but that amendments to that can be moved without notice.
I understood that the motion made by the hon. Minister of Justice was a substantive motion.
That is an amendment to the clause as it stands. Even an addition is an amendment. I have no desire, however, to see the rule pressed.
If I am compelled to rule, I must rule that the amendment of the hon. member for King's, N.B., (Mr. Fowler) is out of order.
The point I take is that you will have to rule on both amendments.

In any case, I think, we can all agree that we do not want three amendments before us at one time, and I do not think any good purpose can be served by my hon. friend pressing that point. When the amendment of the hon. member for Westmoreland is disposed of, my hon. friend can move his. i
But suppose it is adopted ?

I must say that in listening to the discussion to-night concerning this very important measure, I am impressed with the profound ignorance that prevails regarding the location of the line from the Atlantic to the Pacific. I presume that the principal object in view is to find the shortest route. So far as New Brunswick is concerned, I know that the line which keeps to the western part of the province is the most direct line to the seaport of St. John. I have collected figures concerning the different routes through the province of New Brunswick. My hon. friend who represents Victoria, N.B. (Hon. Mr. Costigan) had a Bill before parliament relating to the Quebec and New Brunswick Railway. That railway was to run from Quebec to Connors, where the New Brunswick system of railways terminates, at the extreme north of the state of Maine. The distance from Quebec to Connors I find is 134 miles ; from Connors to Edmundston, 32 miles ; from Edmundston to Grand Falls, 38 miles ; from Grand Falls to Andover, 22 miles; from Andover to Woodstock, 54 miles; from Woodstock to Fredericton, 65 miles ; from Fredericton to St. John, 65 miles; making a total distance from Quebec to St. John of 410 miles. From Quebec to St. John via Chipman is 461 miles. Taking Fredericton as the common point, it is 460 miles via Chipman to St. John, as compared with 410 miles by the valley. From Fredericton to Chipman, there is a line of road surveyed, subsidized and partly built. I suppose that, in the interest of our Nova Scotia friends, rise should be made of that line from Fredericton to Chipman and thence direct to Moncton. That part of the country is well adapted for building a railway. I have been over every foot of the ground myself and therefore can

speak from personal knowledge. A considerable portion of that road will go through the county I represent. There is another fact I would point out. This route, the St. John River Valley, is covered by a road owned by the Canadian Pacific Railway. I do not think it is beyond possibility that the government could acquire that road. It is already being built down the valley of the St. John by the shortest route to the sea, and I think it is a very reasonable proposition that the government should acquire that road, which, I believe, it could do at one-half what it would cost to build through the centre of the province. As regards the line spoken of by the right hon. the First Minister, from Edmundston to Moncton, in a direct line through the centre of New Brunswick, no man can tell what difficulties would be met in its construction.
I have no personal knowledge of the northern part of New Brunswick, but a great many young men who live in my county are employed lumbering in that district, and they all inform me that it is a very rough country indeed. The right hon. gentleman stated to the House that the distance would be 209 miles. That may be correct; but, in view of the difficulties that would have to be encountered, it would be much more expensive to build and operate a road there than the one I have mentioned. The distance to St. John via the Intercolonial Railway is 577 miles. By the St. John valley route it is 410 miles, and by Chipman 401 miles. I think therefore that the suggestion I have made is one that should be adopted and which would satisfy our Nova" Scotia friends. Considerable money could be saved by acquiring that portion of the Canadian Pacific Railway which runs through the valley of St. John and the upper St. John and the government could acquire at the same time the road from Fredericton to Chipman and Moncton. That would affect a saving of money as compared with taking the centre route. My hon. friend from Westmoreland spoke of the difficulty of going down the St. John's valley from Fredericton. There is no such difficulty as he imagines. I know every foot of the route. If we followed the bank of the river all the way down, then difficulties would be met such as he suggests. But I would make a straight line and go down to Gagetown and through the Nerepis country to Westfield country. My hon. friend knows we could get a shorter line by Fredericton going that way than by following the bank of the river.

I think we are wasting our time in this House by this discussion. In the first place, to whom are we talking ? We are talking to a government which does not know what it wants. Have they got an engineer or a map or any one that can tell them what they want ? The other day the right hon. the First Minister read what he Mr. WILMOT.
had to read. Previous to that he had written to the ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) and all that he wrote was not based on any reliable information, tie gave the distances from place to place, and I can prove that his figures were not correct. We are thus all discussing this matter in the dark. Why does not the government postpone this Bill for another six months or a year and in the meantime send out engineers with instructions to run a line from place to place and find out the best route. Until this is done, we are not in a position to intelligently discuss this matter. Each lion, member talks in favour Of his own county or town, and what is the government to do amidst so many contradictory and confusing suggestions and opinions ? Take the hon. gentleman who is promoting this Bill. He has frankly told us that he does not know what to do or what to say. He is simply the promoter of the measure and does not care how it goes. Not long ago I was tailing with a gentleman and he said to me plainly : ' We are in the hands of the Vanderbilts, the Morgans and the Hays.' He told me as plainly as possible-this was six months ago in the city of New York-that the road would be built whatever way Morgan and Hay and Vanderbilt wanted it, and there was no use of our thinking that we had any say in the matter. Is the government going to throw itself into the hands of the Morgans, Hays and Vanderbilts ? If the government allows itself to be dropped into such a mud hole, you will see American engineers over here bringing their own men and running that road wherever they choose; and if anybody else interferes or writes to the government protesting against this as not being right, the government will be as dumb as an oyster, and the first thing we know the road will be built just where Morgan wants it. It is time for us to have a little light thrown on this matter ; and while I have no intention of taking up the time of the House any longer to-night, I shall have something to say later on.
Where does the hon. gentleman gets his figures ?
From the Railway Department.
There is no survey in the department of any such road.
I secured the figures there.
They guessed at them. There are no such figures in the Railway Department.

They are in connection with a railway which was projected,

and Incorporated under the laws of the Dominion.
I know all about it.
I am giving the hon. gentleman some information. The distance from Chaudifire to Connors Station is 130 miles; X won't take off a mile; I won't add a mile.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Emmerson) is right
Order.
I was only agreeing with what the hon. gentleman said.
I must call the hon. gentleman to order.

I thank my hon. friend (Mr. Morin). I want somebody to help me out. The distance from Connors to Ed-mundston is 32 miles; from Edmundston to Nashwaak Bridge is 123 miles; from Nashwaak Bridge to Chipman, 32 miles ; from Chipman to St. John, 66 miles ; total, 383 miles from ChaudiSre to the city of St. John. Now, to St. John from the same point by way of the Intercolonial is 587 miles. That makes a difference of 204 miles. My hon. friend from King's (Mr. Fowler) says that, instead of departing from the main line at Chipman, you should leave the main line at Edmundston and build, down the valley of the St. John, although there is a large system of railways over that route now. I am going to show that the distance would be greater from Chau-diere to St. John by the route the hon. member for King's proposes than by the other. From Cbaudiere to Edmundston is 162 miles. I am now giving you actual distances. From Edmundston to Aroostook Junction is 57 miles ; Aroostook Junction to Woodstock, 53 miles; Woodstock to Fredericton, 60 miles. That makes a total of 332 miles from ChaudiSre Junction to Fredericton over a located railway.
No, 345 miles.

If it makes 345 miles, I am willing to take that. From Fredericton to St. John is 66 miles, making a total of 398 miles from Cbaudiere to St. John by the proposed route of my hon. friend from King's.. By way. of Chipman it is only 383 miles, or 15 miles in favour of the Chipman route. Surely the amendment of my hon. friend will not hold water in the light of these facts.
What is the distance by the Intercolonial from Levis, or from Chaudidre Junction, to St. John?
From Cbaudiere it is 587 miles, and from Levis some miles less.

From L6vis it is 578 miles.
24S

The bridge will cross the river at Quebec, and I think that is the correct point from where to start. The traffic comes across this bridge and the route would start from that point and go through the parishes back of Levis.
Has the hon. gentleman the distance from Fredericton to Moncton ?
I have it from Nashwaak Bridge to Chipman, 32 miles, and from Chipman to Moncton, 51 miles.

I do not know where the hon. member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson, got his figures, and I do not care. If his figures are correct, then the maps that have been furnished officially and have heretofore been regarded as correct, are entirely wrong. Moreover, if the hon. gentleman's figures are correct, the rule of mathematics which declares one side of a triangle to be shorter than the other two sides is all nonsense. It is all very well for the hon. gentleman to talk glibly about the distance from this point to that when there are no engineer's reports on the subject. Of course, we are bound to accept in a parliamentary sense the hon. gentleman's statement. And we do accept it in that sense.
I am glad for even that small measure of credit.

It is quite as much as the hon. gentleman deserves. But if the hon. gentleman will look at the map he will see whether it can be possible that his statements are borne out by the facts. This is an official map issued by the department over which, we .all hope, the hon. gentleman will soon be called to rule. So, we must accept it as being absolutely correct. Also the rule of mathematics to which I have referred and which was taught us in childhood we can hardly deny now. But the acceptance of the hon. gentleman's figures is a denial of both. I do not say that he is making up these figures, but I say that the source from which they are compiled is wrong. It must be wrong, because it is absolutely impossible that a line from Edmundston to St. John-or from St. Leonards, because you have to follow up the line that distance, as I understand, before you branch off-it is impossible that such line to St. John can be longer than if you go across the province of New Brunswick to Chipman, then strike across to Norton on the Intercolonial and back by the Intercolonial. In such a route you are going west, then south-west, and then east.

The distance from Cbaudiere to Connor's Station, 130 miles, is the only section in which there has not been a survey, except the survey made in connection with a railway that was incorporated by this parliament. From Connor's to Edmundston, according to the mil-



eage given by the Canadian Pacific Railway booklet
Your trunk line follows that.

I am giving the figures showing the actual mileage from Edrnund-ston to Nashwaak bridge. From Edmund-ston down to Grand Falls or near there, you have the actual mileage of the Canadian Pacific Railway and the located line. Beyond that you have an actual survey that was made a few years ago, and the mileage was secured by me from data furnished as a result of that survey.
By your proposition you do not go to Fredericton.

I go to Nashwaak bridge, which X think is nine miles from Fredericton. All these distances are absolutely correct from surveys which have been made, or from located lines. So there cannot be any error with respect to the distance of 383 miles. Now as to the 398 miles, I have given a less distance than is given by the hon. member for Sunbury (Mr. Wilmot). He makes the distance over 398 miles. Therefore, it is longer by that route than it is by Chipman, that is, the route that was surveyed a few years ago in connection with the proposed line of railway through the heart of the province.
How far is it from Fredericton to Chipman by the hon. gentleman's figures ?
From Nashwaak it is 32 miles, and 66 miles from that point into St. John.

Sixty-six miles from Chipman to St. John and 32 miles from Nashwaak to Chipman makes 98 miles. Now this Nashwaak bridge is nine miles from Fredericton, and Fredericton is 66 miles from St. John, and 66 miles and nine make 75 miles, and 75 from 98 leaves 23, which is the advantage of the route I speak of. Out of the mouth of the hon. gentleman have I proved that his statement with respect to distance is absolutely incorrect.
You cannot prove the whole by showing that a part is less or more.

The hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Fraser), has made just the statement that a man makes when he jumps in, knowing nothing at all about the case. Now my statement is absolutely correct. The hon. gentleman says that from Nashwaak bridge it is 69 miles to the city of Fredericton. By his own admissions he shows that the route I have been favouring is some 23 miles shorter than the route iie wishes to take to go to St. John by way of Chipman. I cannot understand why the hon. gentleman should be opposing this., Mr. EMMERSON.
It is surely in the interests of Moncton, and it should be the object of the hon. gentleman as a representative from New Brunswick, and it is in the interest of the whole country, to reach an Atlantic port by the shortest possible route. It has been pointed out to the people of St. John that they are going to have all the freight while the passengers will go to Halifax. Well, if you save 23 miles by going to St. John rather than by going to Chipman, why not choose that route ? It is not going to affect our friends from Nova Scotia, it is not going to injure anybody, and it will materially benefit the port of St. John. Therefore, I think the hon. gentleman should withdraw his amendment and allow mine to pass.

The hon. gentleman has referred to the River Valley route, and I pointed out that that route, going down from Woodstock to Fredericton and thence on to St. John, would be a distance of 398 miles. I pointed out that the other route by way of Nashwaak bridge would be
At what point is that bridge-directly opposite Fredericton ?

My hon. friend does not know every foot of that country. There is the covered bridge and the Nashwaak bridge.
Mr. FOWLER, They are both on the Nashwaak river.

They are both on the river. What is known as the Nashwaak bridge is up the Nashwaak river. By this route which is an entirely different route from the river route the difference is fifteen miles. It is a question as to whether the river route or this one is the better. As far as the Nashwaak bridge is concerned it is nine miles from Fredericton. It may be more. It is more than twenty miles, my hon. friend from York, N.B. (Mr. Gibson) states. That does not alter the point raised by myself in respect to these different routes. The Nashwaak bridge route is one and the river route is another. The Nashwaak bridge route is the one that is the shortest.

My hon. friend from Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson), I will not say endeavoured to mislead the committee, but he certainly placed his figures before the committee in a very equivocal manner, saying that he had obtained figures from the Department of Railwayss and Canals showing the distance from Levis to Connors to be 136 miles.
One hundred and thirty.

My hon. friend is a little astray. He should have put the six on. Thesie are the figures given by the promoters.
Mr. EMMERSON My information is 130.

Even these, as the hon. gentleman must know, are short of the true figures. There has never been a survey of that route. Yet, to stand up and give imaginary figures is asking us to accept something that should be taken only with a grain of salt. More than that, no survey for a railway can be run there. It is possible to have a survey for a wagon road, but you cannot have a route 136 miles long or anything like it.
The hon. gentleman is mistaken.

Probably the hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat (Mr. Hughes, Victoria) would be surprised if I could read to him reports of three surveys that have been made all the way from Chaudiere to Edmundston, which is thirty miles beyond Connors.
They have certainly been made, but not to Connors-and not for this route as proposed.
Beyond Connors.
There have been no surveys made for the routes spoken of. I care not what the hon. gentleman says.
The hon. gentleman does not know all that there is in the Railway Department.

A short time ago I asked the government what they contemplated doing for Prince Edward Island in connection with this matter. I received no reply. Whether they desire to treat us with silent contempt or not I do not know, but I am here to raise my voice in favour of the people of Prince Edward Island, and I take the position that the government should do something in connection with this Bill which is now before parliament. We know very well that the company is a mere shadow, that the substance stands behind in the shape of the government, and I would like to ask the government what they contemplated doing for Prince Edward Island in connection with the matter ?

I do not know that there is anything in this Bill showing what the government are going to do for anybody. This Bill is to incorporate a company. There is absolutely not a word in it stating what the government are going to do.
I have an amendment to move in connection with this matter.
There are three amendments before the Chair now.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: An amendment must be relevant to the clause under consideration. This amendment is not relevant.

I must submit to your ruling, but is it the desire of the government that my amendment be overruled ? I invite the Minister of Finance to come to my rescue. He knows very well how matters are in Prince Edward Island, because he has been there, and he has made very strong promises to the people. This company is only the shadow, the government is the substance. In the Bill the company is empowered to acquire railways and build steamships, and it is most unfair to me that I should be ruled out of order, when my amendment is perfectly germane to the whole Bill, and also, I believe, to the clause under discussion.

That ithe amendment be amended by striking out the words ' .or Gravenhurst.'
If you pass this clause without striking out ' Gravenhurst,' it will give power to the Grand Trunk Railway Company to interfere with the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway from Toronto to Sudbury and the James Bay Railway from Toronto to Wahnapitae.
Amendment (Mr. Hughes) negatived.

Inasmuch as there are some radical changes in this Bill, it should comply with the rules of the House and be referred back to the Railway Committee.
Amendment to the amendment agreed to.
That after the word ' Moncton ' on page three, line eleven, the words ' or the city of St. John ' be added in section twelve.

When the hon. gentleman gave notice of this amendment it was understood that the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway were going to build the Quebec and Moncton division. In view of the fact that the government is going to build the section this amendment will come more properly as an amendment to the government measure.
Is it to be unchangeable, like the laws of the Medes and Persians ?

This matter was fully threshed out before the committee and voted down, and I do not

suppose wg will want to discuss it again at this late hour.

The Minister of Finance is* incorrect in stating that I moved this amendment in the Railway Committee. My amendment in the Railway Committee was that it should be built to St. John, and this amendment makes it Moncton or St. John.
I accept the correction, but the substance is the same.
Now that the government is to build that division of the railway, this amendment would come more properly as an amendment to the government measure.

It would do no harm to move it now.
Amendment (Mr. Wilmot) negatived.

One of the reasons given by the Prime Minister for the building of the eastern section of the main line by the government was that it should be thrown open for the use of other railways as well as the Grand Trunk Railway. Does that apply to these branches which are to be built in Ontario, Quebec and New Brunswick by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway? Will other companies have running powers over these branches ?
The contract has no reference to branch lines ; it only refers to the main line. The branches will come under the General Railway Act.
These lines are in no sense branches of this railway as a government road. They are really main hues constructed by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway.

I rather object to discussing the government scheme on this Bill; but I may anticipate the discussion to the extent of saying that they will be branches of a leased line. The Grand Trunk Railway Company have a lease of that line, and as lessees they desire to construct branches.
It seems to me that you might as well say that any road that crosses the Grand Trunk to-day and that is leased by it is a branch. It is not a branch at ail, but another road.
I presume that the interpretation is that the government may also build these and make a present of them to the Grand Trunk Railway Company.

We will think of that by and by.
Mr. McCarthy. The next amendment of which I have given notice is as follows, which I move as an additional clause :

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The directors of the company shall have power to enter into an agreement or agreements with the government of Canada or with commissioners authorized to enter into such agreements on behalf of the government of Canada, respecting the construction and operation of a line of railway, or any portion thereof, to be the property of the government, between the city of Moncton, in the province of New Brunswick, and the city of Winnipeg, in the province of Manitoba, provided, however,^ that such agreement shall not take effect until it has first been approved of by a majority of the votes of the ishareholders of the company, present or represented by proxy at any annual meeting or at a special meeting of the shareholders duly called for the purpose of considering the same.
That is simply conferring upon this company the power to make the lease provided for in the government scheme,
I think the usual course is to require a two thirds vote of the stockholders.
Amendment agreed to.
I wish to add an amendment giving the company all the powers necessary to carry into effect the agreement entered into between them and the government.
Amendment agreed to.

I wish to add a clause of which I have given notice. I beg to move in amendment that the following clause be added :
That all freight originating In Canada and received along the line of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, intended for export across the Atlantic, shall be shipped through Canadian ports, when the route is not otherwise specially engaged by the shipper, and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway shall carry all freight to an eastern Canadian sea port as cheaply as to any American port on the Atlantic sea board.
There is in the agreement, I understand, a clause to that effect, but not in this particular Bill. As the government has seen fit to recognize this proposition as a good one by adopting it in the agreement, no doubt it will be accepted in this Bill.

This is one of several matters which were mentioned before the Railway Committee, .and the view that I took and others was that they were probably matters to be considered in connection with the government contract, but not to insert in a private Bill. The matter has been fully dealt with in the government contract, quite as fully as my hon. friend desires, and I do not see that any good purpose could be served by putting in to this charter the clause he suggests.
Mr. FOWLER, I cannot agree with the hon. gentleman. He claims that the government have provided in the agreement a similar clause, but, we have the absolute right to attach this condition to the charter. The company are asking for a charter, and this

committee has the right to impose any obligation we may consider in the best interest of the country. The hon. gentleman has not given any reason why this amendment should not be accepted.

There are two points in opposition to the hon. gentleman's view. If it were necessary and proper to put this condition into the company's charter, I should prefer other words. The words in the agreement serve the purpose much better than those of my hon. friend, and if we had to put this in the company's charter, I would like to see the words more carefuly chosen. My other objection is that they are out of place in the charter. We cannot reasonably impose this obligation on the company except in connection with government aid. I do not say that we have not the power, but it would be unreasonable to use it. It is only in connection with the government aid that it would be reasonable to impose a condition of this character. And in the Act giving government aid the matter is dealt with.
But supposing the company runs branches from all along the leased line or from the line west of Winnipeg, according to the logic of the minister, this clause would not apply.
As a matter of fact, this does apply to branches too.
Branches constructed without government assistance ?
Without having anything to say as to whether government assistance is given or not.
Before the Bill is reported, may I ask, Mr. Chairman, what became of my amendment ?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: There were two objections to it-one that no notice had been given of it, the other that it was not relevant, in my opinion, to the question under discussion.
Will you allow it to stand as an order for consideration ?
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Hackett) could give notice of it for the third reading.
I will leave it in your hands as a notice, Mr. Chairman.
I think there were some other amendments of which hon. members gave notice.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The mere giving of a notice does not bring these amendments before the committee.
But, Mr. Chairman, you read some that were not moved.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I presented Mr. McCarthy's, because he is the promoter of the Bill. But if hon. members absent themselves from the committee, and expect that I will place their amendments before the committee, they are likely to be disappointed.
Bill, as amended, reported.

speakername: The MINISTER OF MILITIA AND DEFENCE (Hon. Sir F. W. Borden):

speechtext: Mr. BENNETT-by Mr. Hughes (Victoria) ' -asked :

Have any trespasses been made and complained of on the Dokis Indian reserve, French river, during the past five years ? If so, by whom ; and have damages, and to what extent, been paid therefor ? If any amount paid, what disposition was made of same ?

The only trespass of which the department have received notice is a trespass made by the Hardy Lumber Company on the Dokis Indian reserve, French River, during the winter of 1899. The quantity of timber cut was 1,129 saw logs, containing 172,336 feet board measure, for which the department charged and collected $1,034.02 for timber and damages, which sum has been placed to the credit of the capital funds of the Dokis band.
speakername: The MINISTER OF THE INTERIOR (Hon. Clifford Sifton):

speechtext:
Mr. NORTHRUP-by Mr. Hughes (Victoria).-asked :
1.	Has one Rudolph H6tu been lately pardoned ? If so, on whose recommendation ?
2.	For what offences was he sentenced ? For what term was he sentenced ; and how long has he served thereunder ?

1.	Yes. Upon the recommendation of the Minister of Justice founded upon medical certificates to the effect that confinement was rapidly developing tubercular consumption for which unless the patient were released, little could be done in the way of treatment.
2.	Hetu was sentenced for forgery and electoral frauds ; for the first mentioned offence he was awarded twelve months imprisonment ; for the second a fine of $500, or in default of payment, six months imprisonment.
He had served seven months and one day.
speakername: The MINISTER OF JUSTICE (Hon. C. Charles Fitzpatrick) :

speechtext:
In the absence of the Prime Minister, I move that the House go into committee on the following resolution, to-morrow :
Resolved, that it is 'expedient, in connection with the Bill now before this House, respecting the construction of a National Transcontinental Railway, to ratify the agreement set forth in the schedule to the said Bill, entered into on the 28th of July, 1903, between the government and certain persons on behalf of the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company, a company to be incorporated by parliament at the present session thereof, and to authorize the government to do whatever is necessary to give full effect to the said Bill and agreement.
I may say that His Excellency the Governor General has been made acquainted with the subject matter of this resolution, and recommends it to the House.
speakername: The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding).

speechtext: Motion agreed to.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE moved the adjournment of the House.
What will be the business to-morrow ?
